products.title: Monosolenium Tenerum (Pellia) | Bulk Pack
products.body_html:
One portion of moss dresses a stone. Ten or twenty dress a whole piece of driftwood, a moss wall or a carpet. This pack gives you 10 or 20 loose portions of Monosolenium Tenerum (Pellia) in one order, at 40% to 50% less per portion than buying singles.

What You'll Receive

  • 10 Portions: 10 loose portions, each approx. 3" x 3"
  • 20 Portions: 20 loose portions, each approx. 3" x 3"

The same moss as our single Monosolenium Tenerum (Pellia). Size and density may vary slightly with the season.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pellia
  • Scientific name — Monosolenium tenerum
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood, stone or mesh
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to wood, stone or mesh
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. Grows only underwater
  • Propagation — Fragmentation

Grower's Notes

  • Spread it thin. A thin layer over a wide area fills in faster and stays healthier than a thick clump, where the bottom goes brown without light.
  • Pick the pack by the space. 10 portions dress a piece of driftwood or a few rocks; 20 cover a moss wall, a carpet or more than one tank.
  • To attach, press it between two pieces of mesh, tie it on with cotton thread, or glue a thin layer with aquarium-safe gel glue.
  • Trim it often. Regular trims keep moss dense and stop the lower layers from rotting.
  • This one is fully aquatic and cannot be grown out of water, so it is not suited to a terrarium or the dry start method.

Just need one? See the single Monosolenium Tenerum (Pellia).

products.title: Water Mimosa
products.body_html:
Want a plant that reacts when you touch it? Water Mimosa folds its delicate fern-like leaflets inward within seconds of being disturbed, then opens again once left alone. It floats on spongy buoyant stems, forming a soft green canopy — and it is the only plant we sell that moves on its own.

What You’ll Receive

Healthy Water Mimosa plants carefully prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Variants available:

2 Plants – Unrooted
Fresh-cut floating plants without roots.

2 Plants – Rooted
Fresh-cut floating plants with visible developing roots.

10 Plants – Unrooted
Bulk portion of fresh-cut floating plants without roots.

10 Plants – Rooted
Bulk portion of fresh-cut floating plants with visible developing roots.

All plants are carefully selected and shipped fresh to ensure healthy arrival.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Mimosa, also known as Sensitive Water Mimosa
  • Scientific name — Neptunia oleracea
  • Placement — Floating
  • Mature height — 6–8 in above the surface
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 70–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Warmth matters more than most floaters
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also roots in pond margins
  • Propagation — Plantlets along trailing stems

Grower’s Notes

  • The leaf movement is real and repeatable. Touch, vibration or a sudden change in light causes the leaflets to fold within a second or two, reopening over the next few minutes. It is the same mechanism as the terrestrial sensitive plant.
  • Keep the foliage dry. Like other floaters, the leaves sit above the waterline and rot if constantly splashed — aim filter outflow below the surface.
  • It wants warmth. Growth slows markedly at the cool end of its range, so this is a poor choice for an unheated tank.
  • Propagate by separating plantlets that form along the trailing stems and floating them on. It spreads quickly enough to need thinning.
  • Expect folded leaves on arrival. Transit stress makes it close up; it reopens within a day of being floated in stable conditions.

Want to go deeper? Read our guide to the Best Floating Plants for Freshwater Aquariums.

Notes

  • Aquatic plants may experience minor cosmetic changes during shipping due to temperature, handling, and transit time. Leaves may temporarily fold or show slight stress but typically recover quickly once placed in suitable aquarium or pond conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Java Fern Petite Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Java Fern at 2 to 4 inches. Leptochilus pteropus 'Petite' is the dwarf form — narrow, arching leaves on a plant small enough for a nano tank or a bonsai branch, where the standard fern would swamp the layout. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing 2–3 small clumps of Java Fern 'Petite', ready for immediate use in your aquascape.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Petite' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower's Notes

  • Petite stays petite. Unlike a "small size" grade of a large plant, this is a genuinely dwarf cultivar — it will not grow into a standard Java Fern. That is what makes it the right choice for a nano tank rather than a temporary fix.
  • Rinse every trace of gel off before planting. Tissue culture plants arrive in sterile nutrient gel. Any left on the roots feeds a bacterial bloom — rinse under room-temperature water until the roots feel clean, then divide the clumps.
  • Attach the clumps close together. Two or three small clumps look sparse on their own. Grouped on one piece of wood they read as a single established plant within a few months.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots may go into substrate; the green horizontal stem must stay in open water or it rots — the single most common way a Java Fern is killed.
  • Sterile media is the point. No snails, no algae spores, no pesticide residue — which is why this format suits shrimp tanks where a conventionally farmed plant is a real risk.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Java Fern Care Guide.

Notes

Photos are for reference only. Leaf size and shape may vary based on tank conditions. Avoid burying the rhizome—attach only to hard surfaces to prevent rot. Tissue-culture plants may appear smaller than mature aquarium plants and fill out once established.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hygrophila Pinnatifida
products.body_html:
Deeply lobed, fern-like leaves that run bronze to reddish-brown under stronger light — unlike any other stem plant in the hobby. It's also a rheophyte, so it can be planted in substrate or tied to wood and stone like an Anubias.

What You’ll Receive

Choose from a variety of planting formats to suit your layout:

  • Small Bare-Root Plants: Includes 1 small rooted plant, perfect for attaching to driftwood, stones, or décor.
  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 2–3 fresh-cut stems without roots for flexible planting arrangements.
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: 2–3 fresh-cut stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for quick placement.
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: 2–3 fresh-cut stems securely potted in rockwool and a net pot for stability and continued growth.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pinnatifida, Hygrophila Pinnatifida
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila pinnatifida
  • Origin — India
  • Placement — Midground, planted or on hardscape
  • Shipped size — 1 small rooted plant, or 2-3 fresh-cut stems roughly 2-4 in
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Low to medium. It grows in low light; the bronze and red need stronger light
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required if attached to hardscape; nutrient substrate if planted
  • Growth habit — Rheophyte. Plants in substrate or attaches to wood and stone
  • Propagation — Cuttings and side shoots

Grower’s Notes

  • It behaves like two different plants. Tied to wood or stone it creeps sideways and throws vertical shoots like an epiphyte. Planted in substrate it grows taller and greener. Decide which you want before you place it.
  • Pinholes in older leaves mean potassium. This plant is unusually hungry for it and shows the deficiency before anything else in the tank does — treat it as an early warning for your dosing.
  • Bronze and red develop under strong light with iron available. In low light it stays green and healthy — the color is a lighting response, not a health sign.
  • It drops lower leaves as it lengthens. Cut the tops and replant them rather than waiting for the bare stems to fill back in.
  • Also available as sterile Pinnatifida Vitro Culture, and as the compact 'UK' form.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Hygrophila Pinnatifida Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; leaf color, size and form vary considerably with lighting and nutrients. Grown emersed and will transition to submersed growth after planting.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Species on Coco Pad [Grower's Choice]
products.body_html:
Attaching Bucephalandra is the slow part — tying rhizomes to wood, waiting months for them to grip. This is that work already done. A mixed Buce planting grown into a natural coconut-shell pad, ready to drop straight into a tank and move around until it looks right.

What You'll Receive

Grower's Choice Bucephalandra species meaning we will randomly pick the species for you. We do not take requests for specific species or colors. Each order is randomly picked with one mystery species. It may be a bit bigger or smaller in size depending on the variety. We do not label or identify the species.

You will get 1 pad with many rhizomes of Bucephalandra. This is a HUGE-SAVING compared to buying an individual rhizome. We do not take requests for specific species or colors. Each piece is randomly picked, with random varieties and a unique shape that approx. 1x2 inches in size. It may be a bit bigger or smaller in size depending on the variety.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Buce, Bucep
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. (Grower's Choice)
  • Also known as — Tribe Schismatoglottideae, family Araceae
  • Origin — Borneo, Indonesia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground; sits on the substrate or on hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed; the pad sits on top and the rhizomes stay in open water
  • Growth habit — Amphibious epiphyte, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Do not bury the pad. Set it on the substrate or wedge it between rocks. Pushing it under gravel buries the rhizomes underneath, and buried Buce rhizomes rot.
  • It is meant to be moved. The whole point of a pad is that you can lift it, reposition it, or take it out for a water change without disturbing anything else. Use that — try it in a few spots before deciding.
  • Expect roughly an inch of growth a year. Bucephalandra is among the slowest plants sold. The pad will look much as it does now for a long time, which is exactly why it works as a permanent feature.
  • Keep the light low. A slow plant under bright light collects algae faster than it grows new leaves. Low to medium light keeps the leaves clean and holds the blues and purples better.
  • The coconut pad will soften over time. That is normal. By the time it does, the rhizomes have knitted together and hold their own shape.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

Notes

  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation. Unless specific, we don't guarantee aquatic plants will be free of pests, and pesticides, grow emerged or submerge.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hygrophila Kompakt
products.body_html:
Want a Hygrophila that stays in the midground? Hygrophila corymbosa 'Kompakt' is the dwarf cultivar — broad bright green oval leaves on stems with much shorter internodes, so it grows into a dense low bush instead of running for the surface like standard corymbosa.

What You’ll Receive

Your choice of Loose Fresh-Cut Plants, Fresh-Cut Bunched, or Fresh-Cut Potted

  • Loose Fresh-Cut Plants: Includes approximately 3+ loose, fresh-cut stems without roots. Perfect for flexible planting arrangements.
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approximately 3+ fresh-cut stems without roots, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: About 3+ fresh-cut stems without roots, securely potted in a net pot with rockwool, ensuring stability and healthy growth.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Kompakt, also known as Compact Hygrophila
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila corymbosa 'Kompakt'
  • Also known as — Nomaphila siamensis 'Parvifolia'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 3+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 3-6 in
  • Mature height — 4–8 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light keeps the internodes short and the bush tight
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops and side shoots

Grower’s Notes

  • Short internodes are the whole point. Standard Hygrophila corymbosa stretches to 20 inches and beyond with wide gaps between leaf pairs. 'Kompakt' packs them close, which is why it holds a hedge shape where the parent plant does not — and why it fits a 10-gallon tank that the parent would swamp.
  • Light keeps it compact. Under weak light the internodes lengthen and it loses the dwarf habit — trimming won't bring it back.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Each cut forces side shoots, which is how a few stems become a solid midground block.
  • Root tabs help noticeably. It draws from both roots and water column, and leaf size drops in inert gravel.
  • Also available as sterile Kompakt Vitro Culture.

products.title: Hottonia Palustris Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
A temperate plant in a tropical catalog. Hottonia palustris — Water Violet — grows soft feathery lime-green leaves in whorls that read almost like snowflakes along the stem. It is European rather than tropical, and it prefers water at the cooler end of the range, which makes it one of the few genuinely good stem plants for an unheated or lightly heated tank. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® (tissue culture) format.

What You'll Receive

Healthy Hottonia Palustris Vitro Culture plants grown by Aquarium Plants Factory®. Each 4-inch tissue culture bag contains multiple sterile plantlets ready to be separated and planted.

  • 1 Bag — ideal for small aquascapes or accent planting
  • 5 Bags — great for filling midground areas
  • 10 Bags — perfect for larger aquascapes or dense planting layouts

All tissue culture plants are lab-grown, pest-free, and safe for shrimp tanks.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Violet
  • Scientific name — Hottonia palustris
  • Also known as — Featherfoil, Water Yarrow
  • Origin — Europe and western Asia
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — 4-inch bag of small plantlets
  • Mature height — 6–14 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Not required. It grows fuller and denser with it
  • Water — 60–75°F · pH 6.0–7.0. It prefers cooler water than most tropical stems
  • Substrate — Not required. It feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • Keep it cool. This is a European species, not a tropical one. It performs best between 60 and 75°F and thins out in a warm discus or heavily heated tank. That makes it a useful choice for an unheated room-temperature aquarium, where most stem plants sulk.
  • Trim to build the bush. Left alone it grows as single stems. Topping triggers branching, and repeated trimming is what produces the dense feathery clusters it is bought for.
  • Rinse the gel off and separate the plantlets before planting, spacing them an inch apart. Fine whorled foliage shades itself when planted as a clump.
  • Dose the water column. It takes most of what it needs through its foliage rather than its roots.
  • The pale lime-green sits well against darker or broader-leaved plants — it reads as light rather than color, which is a different kind of contrast from a red stem.

Notes

  • Appearance, size, and coloration may vary depending on growing conditions and season. Tissue culture plants may initially appear small but will quickly establish and grow once planted in aquarium conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hygrophila Pink Chai Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want neon pink rather than red? Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai' carries vivid pink through its stems and narrow elongated leaves — a color no other stem plant in our range produces. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format, free of snails, algae and pesticide residue.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple Hygrophila Pink Chai plantlets, ready for rinsing, acclimation, and planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Chai
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai'
  • Also known as — Hygrophila sp. 'Pink Chai', Hygrophila sp. 'Chai', Hygrophila Pink Lady
  • Origin — Natural hybrid of Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia', found at South Island Aquarium in Singapore
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light intensifies the pink
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Sensitive to sudden changes
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Stability matters more than intensity. Pink Chai reacts to sudden shifts in parameters more than most Hygrophila. A steady tank produces better color than a heavily dosed one that swings.
  • Occasional stems revert. The hybrid is stable and cuttings normally come true pink, but a stem may sometimes return to the reddish-brown of the parent Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia'. That is the hybrid behaving normally, not a mislabeled plant — remove reverted stems if you want the stand to stay uniformly pink.
  • Divide the cup into small clumps and plant them a little apart. Tissue culture stock establishes faster with space around it.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • Trim regularly and replant the tops. Topping forces branching, which is what turns a few stems into a block of color.

Prefer rooted plants? See Hygrophila Pink Chai (Small Size) or the standard size.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Hygrophila Chai Care Guide.

Notes

  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ammannia Senegalensis
products.body_html:
Copper and orange, not just red. Ammannia senegalensis runs through a wider color range than most red stems — fiery red through copper into orange, on narrow pointed leaves that curl slightly at the edges. Native to West Africa, and one of the faster-growing red plants once it settles.

What You’ll Receive

  • Available as:
  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approx. 5 unrooted stems, loose for planting or propagation
  • Bunched Plants: Approx. 5 unrooted stems bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approx. 5 unrooted stems planted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Senegal Ammannia
  • Scientific name — Ammannia senegalensis
  • Origin — West Africa
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Color is a light response
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • In a low-tech tank it stays green. The red is produced under strong light with CO₂ — without both, you get a perfectly healthy green plant. Worth knowing before you buy it for color.
  • Leaves curl and twist when growth is fast; that's normal for the species, not a deficiency.
  • Trim the tops and replant them. Cuttings color up faster than the stumps regrow.
  • Plant stems individually an inch apart. Bunched, the lower stems shade out and drop leaves.
  • It feeds at the roots as well as the water column, so root tabs plus regular dosing beat either alone.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ammannia Care Guide.

products.title: Anacharis
products.body_html:
New tank battling algae, or a pond that needs oxygenating? Anacharis is the workhorse. It grows fast enough to strip nitrate before algae can use it, tolerates cold water down to 60°F, and asks for nothing but light — no CO₂, no substrate, no fuss.

What You’ll Receive

You’ll receive approximately 6 fresh Anacharis stems in the format of your choice:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Loose, freshly trimmed stems
  • Bunched Plants: Fresh-cut stems bundled with foam and lead weight
  • Potted Plants: Fresh-cut stems planted in rock wool inside a net pot

All plants are submerged-grown and hand-selected for health and quality.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Anacharis, Brazilian Waterweed, Elodea
  • Scientific name — Egeria densa
  • Placement — Background, or floating as an oxygenator
  • Mature height — 12–24 in and beyond
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. Close to unkillable in the right state
  • Light — Low to medium is plenty
  • CO₂ — Not required! It grows fast enough without
  • Water — 60–82°F · pH 6.5–8.5, and it handles hard alkaline water easily
  • Feeding — Root and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings; snap a stem and replant it

Grower’s Notes

  • It works planted or floating. Floating stems grow fastest and strip the most nitrate, which is why it is the classic new-tank and pond plant — planting it is optional.
  • It handles cold. At 60°F it keeps growing when tropical stems stall, making it one of the few plants suited to unheated tanks and outdoor ponds.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Lower stems go bare as they age; cut the healthy top few inches and discard the base rather than waiting for it to refill.
  • Brittle on arrival is normal. Stems snap easily in transit — every fragment with a node will root and grow, so plant the pieces rather than binning them.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; stem length and leaf density vary with lighting and growing conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cabomba Furcata
products.body_html:
Fine, feathery whorls in pink to reddish-purple — the most delicate texture of any red stem plant, and the reason it's worth the trouble. It is genuinely demanding: high light and pressurized CO₂ are what keep it from unraveling.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as loose Fresh-cut plants, Bunched plants, or Potted plants
  • Fresh-cut plants: Approx. 6 stems, loose fresh-cut stems without root
  • Bunched plants: Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, bundled with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants: Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, potted with net pot and rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Cabomba, Fanwort
  • Scientific name — Cabomba furcata
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–6.8
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • This is the least forgiving red stem in common cultivation. Without strong light and pressurized CO₂ the whorls thin, the stems go bare from the bottom, and it falls apart within weeks.
  • It wants soft, acidic water. Above pH 7 it struggles regardless of how good the light and CO₂ are.
  • Plant stems individually, an inch or so apart. Bunched together they shade each other and rot in the middle.
  • Stable conditions matter more than rich ones. It sheds whorls after water changes that swing temperature or chemistry sharply.

Notes

  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Samolus Parviflorus Red
products.body_html:
Want red without the usual difficulty? Samolus parviflorus 'Red' forms low compact rosettes that turn deep red when grown submerged — and unlike most red plants, it does not demand pressurized CO₂ and extreme light to get there.

Enhance your aquarium with our versatile selection of high-quality aquatic plants, available in three convenient formats:

  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approximately 1-2 fresh-cut stems without roots, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: About 1-2 fresh-cut stems without roots, securely potted in a net pot with rockwool, ensuring stability and healthy growth.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Samolus Red, also known as Red Lettuce
  • Scientific name — Samolus parviflorus 'Red'
  • Also known as — Lysimachia parvifolia 'Red'
  • Origin — Limestone rivers of South China (Guangxi)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground

Care

  • It prefers cooler water than most. At 65–78°F it sits below the usual range, so it does better in a room-temperature tank than a warm one.
  • It comes from limestone rivers, so hard water is no obstacle — useful if your tap water has defeated other red plants.
  • Propagate by separating side shoots. Each rosette establishes independently, so a couple of plants become a patch over a season.

products.title: Christmas Moss
products.body_html:
Want a moss with actual structure rather than a green tangle? Christmas Moss grows in flat, triangular fronds that branch like tiny fir boughs, holding a defined shape as it fills in. It's the moss aquascapers reach for when the moss itself is meant to be seen.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small loose portion, approx. 2" x 2" in size
  • Perfect to attached to driftwood, rock, or stone

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Christmas Moss, Xmas Moss
  • Scientific name — Vesicularia montagnei
  • Also known as — Taxiphyllum sp. 'Christmas', Vesicularia sp. 'Christmas'
  • Placement — Midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner to keep, though slower to establish than Java Moss
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light brings algae it grows too slowly to shed
  • CO₂ — Not required! It simply branches denser and faster with it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation; every trimmed piece grows on

Grower’s Notes

  • Cooler water is what produces the true Christmas shape. Above roughly 78°F the fronds grow looser and longer and it starts to look like ordinary Java Moss — the tight triangular branching is a cool-water trait.
  • Tie it on thin and let it thicken. A thick pad shades and rots underneath long before the surface fills in, and Christmas Moss is too slow to recover from that quickly.
  • Trim the surface every few weeks once established. Cutting forces branching, which is what keeps the frond shape crisp instead of stringy.
  • Gentle flow keeps it clean. The dense fronds trap detritus in still water, and a silted moss browns from the inside out.

Looking to buy in bulk? Get 10 or 20 portions in one order with our Christmas Moss Bulk Pack and save 40–50% per portion.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Aquarium Moss Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference. Portion shape, density and frond form vary with temperature and growing conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hornwort
products.body_html:
Want a plant that fights algae for you? Hornwort grows without roots, floating or tucked into decor, and strips nutrients from the water fast enough to starve algae out. It also releases compounds that suppress algae directly — one of very few aquarium plants that does.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual, loose-cut stems without root

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Hornwort, Coontail
  • Scientific name — Ceratophyllum demersum
  • Placement — Floating or background
  • Mature height — 10–20 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 64–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. It has no roots and feeds entirely from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic. Cannot be grown emersed
  • Propagation — Stem cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • It has no roots and never will. Those pale threads are modified leaves, not roots — planting the base in substrate just rots it. Let it float, or wedge a stem between rocks or wood to anchor it.
  • Expect needle drop on arrival and after any big change. Hornwort sheds when conditions shift and regrows within a week or two. The mess is temporary; keep the firm green stems.
  • It tolerates cold. Comfortable from 64°F, which makes it one of the few plants that works in an unheated tank, a goldfish tank or a pond.
  • Trim and replant tops, discard bare stems. Like most fast stems, the lower section goes bare and does not refoliate.
  • It grows fast enough to shade everything below. Thin it every week or two rather than letting the mat close over.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Hornwort Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference. Hornwort is a delicate, rootless plant and may shed some needles during shipping or after introduction — this is normal and it will regrow quickly under stable conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Micranthemum Glomeratus (Pearl Weed)
products.body_html:
Want one plant that can be a carpet or a hedge? Pearl Weed does both — trimmed low it creeps sideways into a fine bright-green mat, left alone it grows upright into a bushy column. Few plants change role that completely depending on how you cut them.

You may know it as Micranthemum micranthemoides or Hemianthus micranthemoides. Those are the same plant — see the note below.

What You’ll Receive

Enhance your aquascape with our premium-quality Micranthemum glomeratus, available in three flexible planting formats:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approx. 6+ unrooted, loose fresh-cut stems – flexible for custom layout
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approx. 6+ unrooted stems bundled with foam and plant weight for easy placement
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: Approx. 6+ unrooted stems securely potted in a net pot with rockwool for stable growth

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pearl Weed, also known as Pearl Grass, Baby Tears
  • Scientific name — Micranthemum glomeratus
  • Also known as — Micranthemum micranthemoides, Hemianthus micranthemoides (both outdated)
  • Origin — Florida
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 2-4 in
  • Mature height — 2–4 in trimmed, taller left upright
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Why two scientific names?

Pearl Weed was sold for decades as Micranthemum micranthemoides (also written Hemianthus micranthemoides), and most aquarists still know it by those names.

Micranthemum micranthemoides was a real species from the tidal river margins of the eastern United States. It has not been recorded in the wild since the 1940s and is considered extinct. The plant circulating in the hobby under that label was correctly identified in 2011 as a different, living species — Micranthemum glomeratus, from Florida.

So the plant you receive is Micranthemum glomeratus: the same Pearl Weed you have always bought, correctly named.

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. More light gives tighter, denser growth
  • CO₂ — Not required. It carpets faster with it, but does not need it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient substrate makes a visible difference
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Trimming decides what plant you get. Cut it back repeatedly and it branches sideways into a carpet. Leave it and it climbs into a soft green bush. Decide which you want before planting, because the two need different spacing.
  • Don't bury the stems deeply. They are fine and rot if pushed too far into substrate — plant just enough to hold them.
  • Replant the trimmings. Cut tops root readily at the nodes, so one portion fills a foreground over a couple of months at no extra cost.
  • In a nano tank its tiny leaves work as a background filler as well as a carpet — unusual flexibility for a single species.

Prefer the sterile format? See Pearl Weed Vitro Culture, free of snails and algae.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Micranthemum Care Guide.

Notes

  • Images shown are sample representations only. Live plants may vary in size, color, and form based on growing conditions. Unless stated otherwise, plants may arrive in emersed form and are not guaranteed to be pest- or pesticide-free.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Echinodorus Red Flame
products.body_html:
Red without a red stem plant. Echinodorus 'Red Flame' carries broad green leaves scattered with bold red speckling and mottling — color that arrives as pattern rather than a solid block, and on a sturdy rosette plant that needs no trimming regime to keep it. Where red stems demand constant topping, a sword just sits there and holds the color.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 1–2 individual bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 1–2 plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 1–2 plants rooted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Flame Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Red Flame'
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10–16 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light intensity sets how strongly the red speckling shows
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient substrate and root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Feed it at the roots or don't bother. Swords pull most of their nutrition from the substrate. Liquid dosing alone gives you a pale, stalled plant; root tabs under the crown give you the speckling.
  • Expect the first leaves to melt. Nursery plants grow emersed, and the emersed leaves die back after planting. The second flush is the one that shows the pattern.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level. Burying it rots the plant.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A mature plant sends up an inflorescence carrying plantlets along its length. Let each root and grow three or four leaves, then cut it free and plant it separately.
  • Give it room. At 10–16 inches with broad leaves, one plant will shade a surprising area, so treat it as a focal point rather than a filler.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword (Echinodorus) Care Guide.

Notes

  • Color intensity will vary depending on light, nutrients, and water conditions. Older leaves may melt after planting; new growth will adapt to aquarium conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Undulatus Red Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Wavy edges, bronze-red leaves. Cryptocoryne undulatus 'Red' — the wavy leaf crypt — grows narrow, strongly undulating leaves that color reddish to bronze under decent light and nutrients. Movement in the leaf edge plus warm color, on a plant that asks for neither CO₂ nor strong lighting. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture package with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Package size: Approx. 4 inches
  • Sustainable growth aquarium plants species
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Undulatus Red Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne undulatus 'Red'
  • Also known as — Water trumpet, Wavy leaf crypt
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 3–5 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. More light and nutrients deepen the red
  • CO₂ — Not required

products.title: Micranthemum Monte Carlo
products.body_html:
Tried HC Cuba and watched it float away? Monte Carlo is the carpet that stays put. Small round bright green leaves creep across the substrate on runners, and it roots far more securely than HC — which is why it has largely replaced it as the default carpet plant.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Monte Carlo, MC, New Large Pearl Grass
  • Scientific name — Micranthemum tweediei 'Monte Carlo'
  • Origin — Argentina and Uruguay
  • Placement — Foreground carpet
  • Shipped size — Approx. 8+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up

Care

  • Substrate — Required. Fine nutrient substrate holds the stems best
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners — trim and replant

Grower’s Notes

  • Plant small portions an inch apart, not one clump. It closes the gaps by runner faster than you expect, and spacing is what gives you an even carpet instead of a lumpy one.
  • Push the stems in properly. Monte Carlo roots well once anchored, but freshly cut stems have no roots yet and will lift if the substrate is coarse — fine aquasoil holds them best.
  • Trim once it reaches an inch. An untrimmed mat thickens, shades its own base, and eventually lifts off the substrate in sheets.

products.title: Myriophyllum Mattogrossense
products.body_html:
Myriophyllum mattogrossense is one of the finest-textured background plants available — bright green feathery whorls on slender stems that move with the current. It fills a back wall faster than almost anything else, which is both the appeal and the thing to plan for.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 6 individual, loose-cut stems without root
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 6 stems without root bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 6 stems without root potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mattogrossense Milfoil
  • Scientific name — Myriophyllum mattogrossense
  • Also known as — Green Milfoil, Brazilian Milfoil
  • Origin — Mato Grosso, Brazil
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.0
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil helps, but it feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It feeds from the water, not the substrate. Root tabs do little here. Consistent water column dosing — macros and iron — is what keeps the whorls dense and the green bright.
  • Low light makes it leggy, not dead. Under weak lighting the internodes stretch and the feathering thins out. That is a light problem, not a nutrient one.
  • Fast growth means it shades its neighbors. At eight to sixteen inches and growing quickly, it will overtop anything planted in front of it within weeks. Trim on a schedule rather than when it looks untidy.
  • Handle it gently — the foliage is brittle. Fine whorls shed easily when pulled through water or gravel. Plant stems individually with tweezers rather than pushing a bunch in by hand.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Lower stems go bare as the canopy thickens. Cutting the top few inches and replanting them keeps a background even and doubles your stem count.

  • Myriophyllum mattogrossense is a fast-growing plant that may require regular trimming to prevent shading other plants. Under low light, stems may become leggy.

products.title: Java Fern Latifolius
products.body_html:
The widest leaf in the genus. Latifolius means broad-leaved, and this Java Fern earns it — flat, expansive blades on an upright plant that reaches over a foot. Where narrow-leaf forms give a scape fine texture, this one gives it mass.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 3+ leaf portion, loose rhizome
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 3+ leaf portion bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 3+ leaf portion, potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Latifolius Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Latifolius' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground to background, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 8-14 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5, soft to moderately hard
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower's Notes

  • Big leaves are efficient coverage. Java Fern is priced per plant, not per area. On a large piece of wood, one Latifolius covers ground that would take three or four narrow-leaf plants — and it does it without CO₂ or bright light.
  • Broad leaves catch more light, so shade matters more. The wide blade intercepts everything above it, which is good for coverage and bad for algae. Keep it out of the brightest part of the tank and the leaves stay clean.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots may go into substrate; the green horizontal stem must stay in open water or it rots — the single most common way a Java Fern is killed.
  • Wipe the leaves at water changes. A large surface on a slow plant collects debris it cannot shed. A gentle thumb-and-finger wipe every few weeks keeps it dark green.
  • Black spots on old leaves are baby plants, not disease. Leave a spotted leaf in place until each plantlet has roots and two or three leaves, then detach and attach it elsewhere.

Looking to buy in bulk? Get 10 or 20 plants in one order with our Java Fern Latifolius Bulk Pack and save 40–50% per plant.

products.title: Giant Duckweed
products.body_html:
Duckweed you can actually remove. Spirodela polyrhiza has fronds several times the size of common duckweed and much longer trailing roots — which means it nets out in sheets instead of scattering, while still delivering the fast nutrient export and surface shade floaters are bought for.

Plants are carefully harvested and packed to ensure they arrive fresh and ready to add directly to your aquarium or pond.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Giant Duckweed
  • Scientific name — Spirodela polyrhiza
  • Placement — Free-floating on the surface
  • Size — Fronds roughly 0.2–0.4 in across
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium

  • Water — 65–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5

  • Surface flow packs it into corners where it rots. Aim filter returns downward or add a floating ring.
  • Thin it at every water change or it seals the surface and starves plants below of light.
  • Common duckweed often travels with floating plants — check a new portion before adding it if you're keeping the tank Lemna-free.

products.body_html:
Variegation on the toughest stem plant there is. Bacopa monnieri 'Marble' marbles the thick rounded leaves of common Moneywort in green and white — the pattern of a collector's plant on a species famous for surviving anything.

What You'll Receive

  • Scientific name — Bacopa monnieri 'Marble'
  • Also known as — Bacopa Marble, Bacopa Variegated, Marble Water Hyssop
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is pantropical
  • Placement — Midground to background

Care

products.title: Proserpinaca Palustris 'Cuba' (Mermaid Weed) Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
The leaves change shape, not just color. Proserpinaca palustris 'Cuba' — Mermaid Weed — arrives with smooth, plain green foliage from emersed growth, then produces finely toothed, needle-like leaves once submerged, warming to copper, orange and red under strong light. Few aquarium plants alter their form this completely, and the serrated texture is unlike anything else in a planted tank. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® (tissue culture) format.

What You'll Receive

  • 1 Pack Vitro Culture® (4-inch bag) containing multiple young plantlets
  • Each sterile culture can be gently separated into several individual plants ready for planting throughout your aquarium

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mermaid Weed
  • Scientific name — Proserpinaca palustris 'Cuba'
  • Also known as — Cuba Mermaid Weed
  • Origin — North and Central America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — 4-inch bag of small plantlets, smooth-leaved on arrival
  • Mature height — 6–14 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light intensity drives both the serration and the copper-red
  • CO₂ — Recommended for the best color and compact growth
  • Water — 65–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient substrate, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Smooth leaves emersed, serrated submerged
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • Smooth leaves on arrival are correct. Emersed-grown Mermaid Weed has plain, untoothed foliage and looks nothing like the photographs. The serrated needle-like form appears only on new submerged growth — give it several weeks before judging it.
  • Light does two jobs here. It drives the copper-red color, and it also sharpens the serration. Under weak light the plant grows but stays green with softer, less defined leaf edges — losing both of the things it is bought for.
  • Rinse the gel off and separate the plantlets before planting, spacing them an inch apart. Planted as a clump the lower stems shade out.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Cuttings color and serrate faster than the stumps regrow.
  • It pairs well with Rotala and Ludwigia — similar warm tones, completely different leaf texture, which is what makes the grouping work.

Notes

products.title: Rotala Vietnam Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Rotala wallichii 'Long Leaf' (Rotala Vietnam) in Vitro Culture® – Fine-Leaved, Fast-Growing Stem Plant for Elegant Aquascaping

Rotala wallichii 'Long Leaf', commonly referred to as Rotala Vietnam, is a visually delicate and fast-growing aquarium stem plant prized for its fine, needle-like foliage and graceful vertical growth.   • Common Name: Rotala Vietnam

  • Leaf Shape: Ultra-fine, needle-like leaves with extended length

  • Coloration: Transitions from lush green to orange or reddish tones under high light

  • Growth Habit: Upright, bushy stem growth ideal for layering

products.title: Echinodorus Yellow Sun
products.body_html:
Most swords are green. 'Yellow Sun' comes through yellow-green, sometimes with orange or light red at the edges under stronger light — heart-shaped leaves that read as a warm patch rather than another block of dark foliage.

What You'll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our fresh, high-quality plants, available in convenient formats:

  • Loose Bare-Root Plants: Includes approximately 1-2 loose, bare-root plants, providing flexibility in planting and arrangement.
  • Rooted Bunched: Approximately 1-2 plants, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Rooted Potted: Includes approximately 1-2 plants, potted in a net pot with rock wool, ensuring stability and ease of placement in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Yellow Sun Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Yellow Sun'
  • Also known as — Echinodorus cordifolius 'Yellow Sun', Golden Sun Sword
  • Origin — Cultivated form; parent species from the Americas
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient-rich soil or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Light decides whether it is yellow or just green. Under medium light the leaves lean pale green; stronger light brings out the golden tone and the orange-red edging. This is the one variable worth adjusting if the color disappoints.
  • Root tabs are not optional. Swords take almost everything from the substrate. In inert gravel with liquid dosing alone the yellow washes out to a sickly pale green, which is easy to mistake for a deficiency in the water column.
  • Never bury the crown. Cover the roots and leave the growing point at substrate level. A buried crown rots from the center and does not recover.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A mature plant sends up an inflorescence carrying plantlets along its length; let each root and grow three or four leaves before separating it.
  • Use it against green, not against red. Yellow-green next to red plants muddies both. Set against dark green foliage or wood it does what it is bought for.

products.title: Helanthium Vesuvius (Twisted Chain Sword)
products.body_html:
Vallisneria with a twist — literally. Helanthium bolivianum 'Vesuvius' grows narrow ribbon leaves, roughly 4 mm wide, that spiral tightly as they rise from a low rosette. Selected from a mutation of H. bolivianum 'Angustifolius' at the Oriental nursery in Singapore and in the trade since 2006.

What You'll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our fresh, high-quality plants, available in convenient formats:

  • Loose Bare-Root Plants: Includes approximately 1–2 loose, bare-root plants, providing flexibility in planting and arrangement.
  • Rooted Bunched: Approximately 1–2 plants, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Rooted Potted: Includes approximately 1–2 plants, potted in a net pot with rock wool, ensuring stability and ease of placement in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Vesuvius Twisted Chain Sword, also known as Corkscrew Sword
  • Scientific name — Helanthium bolivianum 'Vesuvius'
  • Also known as — Echinodorus 'Vesuvius' (the older name)
  • Origin — Cultivated selection, Singapore; the species is native to South America
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 3-6 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — fine gravel, sand or aquasoil with root tabs.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners. Unlike the true Echinodorus swords, chain swords genuinely do spread under the substrate.

Grower's Notes

  • It arrives straight and twists later. We grow it emersed, where the leaves are broader, shorter and barely curled. The tight spiral only develops on submerged growth — so the plant in the bag will not look like the photograph, and that is expected.
  • This one really does send runners. Chain swords are Helanthium, not Echinodorus: they spread under the substrate, rooting daughter rosettes a few inches from the parent. Leave each runner attached until the daughter has its own roots, then lift and move it.
  • Feed the roots. Root tabs or aquasoil under the planting area do far more than liquid dosing for a plant that feeds this way.
  • Use it where the movement shows. The spiral reads as motion in open water or gentle flow. Crowded between broad-leaved plants the effect disappears and a plain chain sword would do the same job.
  • Expect emersed leaves to melt back. Remove them once they yellow — it encourages the submerged rosette to fill in faster.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Helanthium Chain Sword Care Guide.

Notes

This plant is shipped in its emersed form. Upon submersion, the leaves will gradually transition into their final form—narrow, upright, and tightly twisted. Older emersed leaves may melt back, which is normal. Remove any unsightly leaves to encourage healthy submerged growth.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia'
products.body_html:
Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia' does not behave like the rest of its genus. Instead of racing to the surface it stays low and branches sideways, building compact bushes of narrow, needle-shaped leaves in bronze, brown and deep red. It is the rare Hygrophila you plant in the middle of a tank rather than behind everything.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia' cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

  • Fresh Cut Plants: Approximately 6 loose, fresh-cut stems without roots.
  • Fresh Cut Bunched: Approximately 6 stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Fresh Cut Potted: About 6 stems potted securely in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Araguaia Hygrophila
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia'
  • Also known as — Hygrophila Araguaia, Hygrophila 'Chai' relative
  • Origin — Collected from the Araguaia river basin, Brazil; the species itself is native to East Asia
  • Placement — Midground
  • Mature height — 4-10 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It branches instead of climbing. Most Hygrophila needs constant topping to stay in the midground. Araguaia naturally throws side shoots and stays compact, so a planted group thickens on its own with far less trimming.
  • CO₂ changes the leaf shape. Without injection the leaves are broader and the growth looser. With it, they narrow into the fine needle form and the bush tightens — the difference is visible rather than subtle.
  • Color sits between bronze and red. This is not a scarlet plant. Under medium light with steady iron dosing it holds a brown-red tone that reads as depth against green neighbors, which is exactly what makes it useful.
  • Expect melt in the first two weeks. Emersed-grown stems drop most of their original leaves after planting. Leave the stems in place — the submersed growth that follows is the form you want.
  • Plant it where a stem plant would normally be too tall. At four to ten inches it fills the awkward gap between a carpet and a background hedge, which few red plants do well.

Notes

  • Images are for reference only; actual plants may vary in size, color, and fullness
  • Plants may be grown emersed and will transition once submerged
  • Minor melting during acclimation is normal
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Brazilian Pennywort Marble
products.body_html:
Brazilian Pennywort is already one of the easiest stem plants sold. The marbled form keeps that and adds cream and pale green streaking across those round, lily-pad leaves — rare-looking foliage on a plant that grows fast enough to fill space in weeks.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Brazilian Pennywort Marble cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

  • Fresh Cut Plants: Approximately 4 fresh-cut stems without roots.
  • Fresh Cut Bunched: Approximately 4 stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Fresh Cut Potted: About 4 stems potted securely in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Marble Brazilian Pennywort
  • Scientific name — Hydrocotyle leucocephala 'Marble'
  • Also known as — Hydrocotyle leucocephala 'Variegated'
  • Origin — Central and South America
  • Placement — Midground, or left floating
  • Mature height — 8-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; also feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious creeping stem
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • Variegated does not mean difficult here. Pennywort grows fast enough to carry the loss of chlorophyll without slowing down. It stays a beginner plant — the marbling costs you nothing in difficulty.
  • Solid green stems will appear. Any variegated plant can revert, and green growth is more efficient so it spreads if left. Cut reverted stems out at the base as you spot them.
  • It grows in three directions. Planted it climbs, floated it spreads across the surface, and laid against hardscape it creeps. Decide which you want and trim to enforce it — left alone it does all three at once.
  • Every node roots. Cut anywhere and both halves grow. Four stems become a dense patch within a couple of months with nothing more than scissors.
  • Floating stems shade what is below. The leaves are broad and they cover a surface fast. Keep it trimmed back if there is anything light-hungry underneath.

Notes

  • Live aquatic plants may show minor cosmetic differences due to natural growth variation. Images are for reference only. Some melting or adjustment may occur as the plant transitions to your aquarium environment.

products.title: Bolbitis Difformis
products.body_html:
Want the Bolbitis look in a small tank? Bolbitis heteroclita var. difformis is the miniature one — finely divided lacy fronds on a compact rhizome, where the African Water Fern grows to over a foot. It attaches to wood and stone and stays in scale with a nano layout.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Bolbitis heteroclita var. difformis cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Bare-root Plants: Approximately 1–2 plants with loose bare roots rhizome.

Rooted Bunched: Approximately 1–2 plants secured with aquarium-safe foam and a plant weight.

Rooted Potted: Approximately 1–2 plants established in a net pot with rockwool.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Bolbitis, also known as Philippine Bolbitis, Lace Bolbitis
  • Scientific name — Bolbitis heteroclita var. difformis
  • Origin — Philippines
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 3–6 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light means algae on slow-growing fronds
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it fills out faster with it
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also suits high-humidity terrariums
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower’s Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or stone with the rhizome exposed — buried in substrate it rots, and that is how most Bolbitis is lost.
  • Give it flow. This is a rheophyte from shaded Philippine streams, and moderate current keeps the fine fronds clean and moving. Still water lets detritus settle in the foliage.
  • It is slow to start. Expect several weeks before the first new frond, and avoid moving it while it settles.
  • Expect a transition period. It is usually grown emersed, and the first fronds may die back as it converts to submerged growth.
  • Divide by cutting the rhizome, leaving several fronds and some root on each section.

Want the full-size version? See Bolbitis Heudelotii (African Water Fern), which reaches 8–14 in.

Looking to buy in bulk? Get 10 or 20 plants in one order with our Bolbitis Difformis Bulk Pack and pay less per plant.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ozelot Green Sword

  • Also known as — Green Ozelot Amazon Sword

  • Placement — Midground to background

  • Difficulty — Beginner

products.title: Hygrophila Difformis (Water Wisteria) Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
The plant to put in a new tank. Hygrophila difformis — Water Wisteria — grows fast enough to soak up the nutrient surge that feeds early algae, while its finely cut lace-like leaves give a soft texture against broad-leaved plants. Forgiving, quick, and cheap to fill space with. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh Vitro Culture® Hygrophila difformis prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in multiple pack sizes.

Each portion comes in a sealed 4-inch sterile Vitro Culture® bag containing numerous young plantlets grown in nutrient gel.

1 Bag: One 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple healthy plantlets ready for separation and planting.

5 Bags: Five 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags, ideal for filling larger aquascapes or multiple aquariums.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Wisteria
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila difformis
  • Also known as — Synnema triflorum
  • Origin — Indian subcontinent
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10–20 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Stronger light gives fuller, more compact growth
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient substrate or root tabs recommended
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Leaf shape changes and that's normal. Tissue culture plantlets are grown emersed with simple rounded leaves. Submerged, the plant produces the deeply cut lacy foliage it's known for. New buyers often think they've been sent the wrong plant — wait for the second flush.
  • Use it as an algae counter in a new tank. Fast growth means it consumes the nutrients algae would otherwise take while slower plants establish.
  • Trim and replant tops. Every cutting roots within days, so one bag furnishes a background.
  • Space stems an inch apart. Bunched, the lower leaves shade out and drop.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae early on.

products.title: Cardamine Lyrata Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Round leaves on trailing stems, and it likes it cool. Cardamine lyrata — Japanese Cress — creeps rather than stands, sending stems with bright rounded leaves across the substrate and over driftwood. It comes from temperate East Asia and does best between 65 and 75°F, which makes it a useful choice for an unheated or lightly heated tank. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® (tissue culture) format.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold in a 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag, yielding 3–4 healthy plant clusters ready for aquarium planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Japanese Cress
  • Scientific name — Cardamine lyrata
  • Also known as — Cardamine, Chinese Ivy
  • Origin — Temperate East Asia
  • Placement — Midground; trails over hardscape
  • Shipped size — 4-inch bag, approx. 3–4 clusters
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light keeps it compact rather than stretched
  • CO₂ — Not required. It grows well in low-tech tanks
  • Water — 65–75°F · pH 6.5–7.5. It prefers cooler water than most tropical plants
  • Substrate — Not required, though growth improves over a fed base
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Excellent emersed in paludariums and terrariums
  • Propagation — Cuttings — every stem section roots

Grower's Notes

  • Keep it cool. This is a temperate species, not a tropical one. Above about 78°F it stretches, thins and drops leaves. In a room-temperature or lightly heated tank it thrives — which is the opposite of most plants in this catalog.
  • Let it trail rather than planting it upright. The stems creep and drape naturally over wood and rock. Trying to grow it as a vertical stem plant fights the way it wants to grow.
  • Rinse the gel off and separate the clusters before planting, spacing them out so the runners have somewhere to go.
  • Trim regularly. It grows fast and the round leaves look best on young compact growth; older stems bare off at the base.
  • Round foliage is genuinely uncommon underwater, so it reads as contrast against the fine and strap-leaved plants most tanks already have.

Notes

  • As with all aquarium plants, Cardamine lyrata may transition from its emersed tissue culture form to submerged growth. Some initial leaf melt is normal as the plant adapts to your aquarium conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Dwarf Sagittaria Subulata
products.body_html:
Want a carpet you can grow without CO₂? Dwarf Sagittaria is a grass-like rosette that spreads by runner into a dense colony, with its height set by your lighting rather than by the plant. Bright light keeps it low enough for a foreground; in dimmer tanks it stretches upward and reads as midground.

  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed; feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious epiphyte
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue the green horizontal stem to wood or rock and leave it in open water. Buried in substrate it rots — the single most common way Java Fern is killed.
  • Black spots on old leaves are baby plants, not disease. Java Fern reproduces by growing plantlets along the leaf margins. Leave a spotted leaf in place until each plantlet has roots and two or three leaves, then detach and attach it elsewhere.
  • It grows upright, which changes where you use it. Standard Java Fern spreads outward; 'Philippine' holds height. That makes it a background plant in a small tank and a midground one in a large tank.
  • Keep the light modest. It grows slowly enough that strong lighting mostly feeds algae on the fronds. Shaded positions give cleaner, darker leaves.
  • Give it time before judging it. Emersed-grown fronds often brown off after planting. As long as the rhizome stays firm and green, submersed leaves follow — they simply take a couple of months.

products.title: Bolbitis Heudelotii Difformis
products.body_html:
Want the Bolbitis texture without the size? This compact 'Difformis' form grows finely dissected, ruffled fronds on a plant that stays well under a foot — the lacy structure of a full-size African Water Fern, in scale for a smaller tank.

What You’ll Receive

Available in three formats:

  • Bare-Root Plants: 4+ healthy fronds with rhizome, loose for flexible placement
  • Bunched Plants: 4+ fronds tied with foam and weight for easy setup
  • Potted Plants: 4+ fronds rooted in rockwool and net pot for secure anchoring

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Compact African Water Fern, also known as Dwarf Bolbitis
  • Scientific name — Bolbitis heteroclita var. difformis
  • Placement — Midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 4–8 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Low to medium. High light encourages algae on slow-growing fronds
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it fills out faster with it
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5, soft to moderately hard
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Emersed growth needs high humidity
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower’s Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or stone with the rhizome exposed — buried in substrate it rots, and that is how most Bolbitis is lost.
  • Give it gentle to moderate flow. Bolbitis are rheophytes and appreciate current, but this compact form dislikes heavy turbulence — steady rather than strong.
  • It is slow to establish. Expect several weeks before the first new frond, and avoid moving it while it settles.
  • Divide by cutting the rhizome between leaf clusters, leaving several fronds and some root on each section.
  • Pairs naturally with mosses, Anubias and Bucephalandra — all shade-tolerant epiphytes with the same care needs.

Comparing our Bolbitis: the full-size Bolbitis Heudelotii reaches 8–14 in, and Bolbitis Difformis (B. heteroclita var. difformis) is the smallest at 3–6 in.

New to attaching plants? Read our guide on how to attach epiphyte plants to driftwood and rock.

Looking to buy in bulk? Get 10 or 20 plants in one order with our Bolbitis Heudelotii Difformis Bulk Pack and save 40–50% per plant.

Notes

  • As a slow-growing fern, this plant may take time to adjust and establish in new environments. Avoid burying the rhizome in substrate, as it may rot. Attach with thread or glue to wood or rock for best results.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Samolus Parviflorus Red Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Red that stays put. Samolus parviflorus 'Red' grows low, compact rosettes of rounded leaves that turn pink to deep red submerged — no topping, no replanting, no stems falling over. Easier to place than any red stem plant, and it prefers cooler water than most. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as a Vitro Culture® cup in a sealed 4-inch bag:

  • 4-inch Bag: Contains multiple young plants, ready for propagation and planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Samolus, Red Water Pimpernel
  • Scientific name — Samolus parviflorus 'Red'
  • Also known as — Red Lettuce
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 2–6 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Intensity deepens the red
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 65–78°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Note the ceiling — it prefers the cooler end
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Green emersed, red submerged
  • Propagation — Side shoots and separated rosettes

Grower’s Notes

  • It arrives green. Tissue culture plantlets are grown emersed and come out of the bag pale green. The red develops over several weeks of submerged growth — judge the color then, not on arrival.
  • It prefers cooler water than most red plants. At 65–78°F it does better in a room-temperature tank than a warm tropical one.
  • As a rosette it stays where you plant it — far less work than a red stem plant that needs constant topping.
  • Separate side shoots once each has roots of its own; a couple of plants become a patch over a season.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae early on.

Want to go deeper? Read our guide to getting real color from red aquarium plants.

Notes

  • As with most rosette plants, Samolus parviflorus 'Red' may experience a brief adjustment period (known as "melt") after planting. Trim away melted portions and provide stable lighting, CO₂, and nutrients to encourage healthy new growth.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Kedagang Red on Driftwood
products.body_html:
Kedagang Red, also known as Red Godzilla, is among the darkest reds in the Bucephalandra range — long narrow leaves with a leathery texture running deep red through bronze. This version arrives already attached to a nano piece of driftwood, so there is nothing to tie.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a plant on a nano driftwood.
  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Kedagang Red Buce on Driftwood
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Kedagang Red'
  • Also known as — Red Godzilla, Buce Kedagang Red
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Midground; the driftwood sits on the substrate or nestles into hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-5 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Stronger light deepens the red, but also brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow.
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; feeds from the water column.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Set the wood on the substrate, don't push it in. The rhizome is already correctly positioned above the wood. Bury it and it rots, which is the usual way an expensive Buce is lost.
  • Color builds over months. It arrives greener than the photos and darkens as it settles into submerged growth — judge it at three months, not on arrival.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Because the piece is loose you can move it to test placement without disturbing anything else in the tank.
  • Some leaf melt after shipping is normal. The rhizome survives and pushes new submersed leaves within a few weeks.

Godzilla and Kedagang are the same name — the color is what tells them apart. See also Pink Godzilla (Kedagang Pink) and Green Godzilla, which are different plants.

products.title: Hydrocotyle Verticillata Vitro Culture (Pennywort)
products.body_html:
Round leaves held up like small umbrellas. Hydrocotyle verticillata joins each leaf to its stalk at the center rather than the edge, so the foliage stands upright on thin stems instead of trailing flat — a shape nothing else in a planted tank produces. This is the sterile tissue culture version.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture plants with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Bag size: Approx. 4 inches. Yield many small plants
  • Sustainable growth aquarium plants species
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Umbrella Pennywort
  • Scientific name — Hydrocotyle verticillata
  • Also known as — Whorled Pennywort, Whorled Marshpennywort, Shield Pennywort
  • Origin — The Americas
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 4-8 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; also feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious creeping stem
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • Bare stalks with few leaves means not enough light. Under weak lighting the stems stretch upward and the umbrella leaves thin out. Raise the intensity or move it forward rather than dosing more fertilizer.
  • Separate the culture into small clusters. Rinse the gel off and plant a few plantlets per spot, an inch apart. Runners close the gaps far faster than one clump grows outward.
  • Trim at the substrate to hold a boundary. Runners spread quickly and will cross into whatever is planted next to it. A trim every few weeks keeps the patch where you put it.
  • Every node roots. Cut sections anywhere and pin them down with plant weights until they anchor. It is one of the easiest plants in the catalog to multiply.
  • The upright leaf on a central stalk is the identifying feature — useful for telling this apart from the flat-creeping Hydrocotyle tripartita, which is a different plant entirely.
