products.title: Anubias Petite Snow White Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Cream-white marbling on leaves under an inch across. Anubias sp. 'Petite Snow White' is one of the most heavily variegated Anubias in the hobby — and, for exactly that reason, one of the least forgiving. This is the sterile tissue-culture format.

What You'll Receive

  • One (1) Vitro Culture® 4-inch bag of Anubias sp. 'Petite Snow White'
  • Yield: Approximately 3–4 small young plants, ready to plant or attach to hardscape

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite Snow White Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias sp. 'Petite Snow White'
  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Low to medium. Excess light burns the pale tissue and feeds algae — the single most common way this plant is lost.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Improves vigor under otherwise stable conditions.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5. Stability matters more than any particular value.
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte; attaches to wood or stone.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, once well established

Grower's Notes

  • Cream-white tissue carries no chlorophyll, which is what makes this Advanced. The more white a leaf holds, the less energy the plant produces — so it grows very slowly, recovers badly from damage, and cannot outgrow algae on the pale areas. Anubias is famously indestructible; this cultivar is the exception that proves it.
  • It can revert. Heavily variegated Anubias sometimes starts pushing plain green leaves. Remove fully green shoots promptly — green tissue photosynthesizes better and will gradually take the plant over if left.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to wood or stone and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot, and this plant will not grow back from that quickly.
  • Rinse the gel off gently with aquarium or dechlorinated water — not tap — and separate the plantlets before attaching.
  • The sterile format matters more here than on a hardy plant: an algae outbreak arriving with the plant is very hard to clear from white leaves that grow this slowly.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Anubias Care Guide.

Notes

Pictures shown are for reference only. Actual plant size, shape, and variegation pattern may vary depending on growing conditions. This Vitro Culture® bag is sealed for freshness — please follow proper sterilization and acclimation procedures upon opening.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Retrospiralis Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Tall, ribbon-like leaves that twist along their length. Cryptocoryne retrospiralis is one of the few crypts that works as a background plant — it gives a planted tank vertical movement without the trimming a stem plant demands. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

  • 1x Cryptocoryne Retrospiralis Vitro Culture® — grown in 4-inch bag
  • Yields approx. 3–4 healthy young plants ready for planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Retrospiralis Crypt, also known as Spiral Water Trumpet
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne retrospiralis
  • Origin — India
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it speeds establishment
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs under the crown.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed, so it suits paludariums
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • A background plant that does not need cutting. Stem plants reach the surface and then need weekly trimming. Retrospiralis grows to height and stops, which is the entire argument for using a crypt at the back of a low-maintenance tank.
  • Crypt melt is expected and is not failure. Tissue culture plantlets shed their emersed leaves as they convert to submersed growth. Leave the roots undisturbed — new leaves come from the crown within three to six weeks.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level. Bury the roots and leave the growing point exposed. A buried crown rots from the center.
  • Feed the roots and give it depth. A tall crypt needs a deep, well-fed substrate to anchor and fuel 16 inches of leaf. Root tabs or aquasoil; two inches of substrate minimum.
  • It spreads by runner. Once settled it sends up new plants around the mother — leave space behind it and the stand thickens on its own over a year or two.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Cryptocoryne Care Guide.

Notes

Like many Cryptocoryne species, Cryptocoryne retrospiralis may undergo a temporary "crypt melt" when adapting to a new aquarium environment. This is a normal process. Once established, new growth will emerge and the plant will stabilize.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia Glandulosa (Peruensis)
products.body_html:
Want burgundy rather than scarlet? Ludwigia glandulosa runs deep wine-red to purple on narrow lance-shaped leaves held on stiff upright stems. It is one of the darker reds available, and it grows straight up with almost no branching — which makes it unusually easy to place.

You may know it as Ludwigia peruensis. That is a trade name — see the note below.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approx. 6 individual loose-cut stems without root.
  • Bunched Plants: Approx. 6 stems without root, bundled with foam and plant weight.
  • Potted Plants: Approx. 6 stems without root, potted in rockwool and a net pot.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Peruensis, also known as Cylindricfruit Primrose-Willow
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia glandulosa
  • Also known as — Ludwigia peruensis, Ludwigia perennis, Ludwigia cylindrica (all misapplied)
  • Origin — Southeastern United States
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Why several names?

This plant has been sold as Ludwigia peruensis and Ludwigia perennis for years, and both names are still in wide use. Neither is correct — the plant is Ludwigia glandulosa, a species from the wetlands of the southeastern United States, not from Peru.

You are buying the same plant you have always known as Peruensis, correctly named.

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Intensity decides whether you get wine-red or olive-green
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder, hungry for iron
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • It barely branches on its own. Stems grow straight up with minimal side shoots until you cut the main stem — then lateral shoots form. If you want a dense stand rather than isolated poles, topping is not optional.
  • In lower light the leaves go olive-green with red undersides, which is a two-toned effect worth having in its own right. The wine-red only appears under strong light.
  • It sheds lower leaves when light is insufficient. Bare stems near the substrate mean light isn't reaching them, not a nutrient problem.
  • Iron and steady micronutrients matter more here than for most Ludwigia.
  • Often confused with Ludwigia senegalensis, which carries a visible vein pattern this one lacks.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

Notes

  • Pictures shown are sample representations and not the exact plants you will receive. Unless otherwise specified, we do not guarantee aquatic plants will be free of pests or pesticides, nor whether they are grown emersed or submerged.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia Rubin
products.body_html:
Most deep red stem plants demand a high-tech tank before they show any color. Ludwigia Rubin does not. Broad, spade-shaped leaves turn wine red on both surfaces under medium light with no CO₂ at all, which makes it the shortest route to a red midground in a low-tech tank.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Ludwigia Rubin cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats.

  • Fresh-cut Plants: Approximately 6+ loose, fresh-cut stems without roots.
  • Fresh-cut Bunched: Approximately 6+ stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy planting.
  • Fresh-cut Potted: Approximately 6+ stems securely potted in a net pot with rockwool for stability and convenient planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Rubin
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia repens 'Rubin'
  • Also known as — Red Diamond, Ludwigia Ruby
  • Origin — Cultivated form of a North and Central American species
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 inches
  • Mature height — 6-16 inches
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Not required. It reddens without injection, which is the whole point of this cultivar
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • This is the red plant to start with. Most reds need high light and injected CO₂ before they color. Rubin does it on medium light in a low-tech tank — if earlier attempts at a red plant have failed, this is the one that changes that.
  • Both leaf surfaces color up. Unlike Ludwigia repens, which stays green on top and red underneath, Rubin holds red through the whole leaf. That is why it reads as a solid block of color from the front of the tank.
  • Low nitrate deepens it, but do not starve it. Rubin darkens when nitrate is kept modest and iron is dosed consistently. Cutting nitrate to zero stalls the plant instead — aim for lean but present.
  • Trim above a node and replant the cutting. Each cut stem branches into two, so repeated trimming builds a dense red thicket rather than a row of single stems.
  • Emersed stock changes shape after planting. Leaves grown out of water are thicker and often greener. The first submersed leaves are broader and considerably redder, so judge the plant by its new growth.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

Notes

  • Aquarium plants are living organisms and may naturally vary in size, shape, and coloration depending on season, lighting, and growing conditions. Most plants are grown emersed before shipping and will gradually transition to their submerged form after being introduced into the aquarium.

products.title: Alternanthera Reineckii
products.body_html:
The benchmark red stem plant. Alternanthera reineckii — Scarlet Temple, or simply AR — grows broad leaves with green tops and deep red-to-purple undersides on upright bushy stems. It is the plant most people mean when they say they want red in a planted tank, and unlike many red stems it will color without pressurized CO₂.

  • Scientific name — Alternanthera reineckii
  • Also known as — AR, Telanthera rosefolia
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Midground to background

  • Mature height — 8–16 in

  • Difficulty — Intermediate

products.title: Pogostemon Stellatus
products.body_html:

Pogostemon stellatus whorls fine needle-like leaves around the stem so each node opens like a small explosion, and under strong light with CO₂ the whole plant shifts from green through pink and purple into orange. It is one of the most striking stem plants in the hobby and one of the least tolerant of an unstable tank.

  • Scientific name — Pogostemon stellatus
  • Also known as — Eusteralis stellata, Star Pogostemon
  • Origin — Southeast Asia and Australia
  • Placement — Background

  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant top cuttings or side shoots

Grower’s Notes

  • Stability matters more than any single parameter. Stellatus reacts to swings in CO₂, light period or fertilisation faster than almost anything else in the tank — it will drop leaves in a week from a change others shrug off. Set the tank up first, then add this plant.
  • Melt after shipping is normal and can look total. Leave the stems planted; new growth comes from the nodes.
  • Trim the tops and replant them; side shoots from the trimmed stem thicken the group.
  • Plant stems individually an inch apart. Bunched, the lower stems shade out and rot.
  • Want the leaf texture without the demands? Pogostemon Octopus keeps a similar form and stays green, and Pogostemon Deccanensis is a far more forgiving background plant.

  • Pogostemon stellatus is a sensitive species that may melt or lose leaves during shipping or acclimation. Stable parameters, high light, and CO₂ injection are key to long-term success.

products.title: Vallisneria Torta
products.body_html:
Want a corkscrew Val that stays small? Vallisneria torta is the shortest of the twisted Vallisneria — light green, almost translucent spiral leaves reaching only about 8 inches, which makes it the only one that works in a nano tank or a genuine foreground.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as Bare-root Plants, Bunched plants, or Potted plants
  • Bare-root plants | approx. 2-3 loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunched plants | approx. 2-3 rooted plants with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants | approx. 2-3 rooted plants with net pot and rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Torta Val, also known as Corkscrew Val
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria torta
  • Also known as — Vallisneria asiatica var. biwaensis (the identity is not firmly settled, and nurseries sell it as Torta)
  • Origin — Asia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 2-3 plants, roughly 3-6 in
  • Mature height — 4–8 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Brighter light tightens the spiral
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Tolerates hard, alkaline water well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • This is the small one. Most Vallisneria run to the surface and trail along it. Torta tops out around eight inches, so it works as a foreground or midground group and suits nano tanks — the only twisted Val that does.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut — remove whole leaves at the base instead.
  • Runners travel fast. Pull unwanted plantlets by hand rather than cutting them.

Choosing between our twisted Vallisneria

  • Vallisneria torta (this plant) — shortest, 4–8 in, midground and nano tanks.
  • Vallisneria americana 'Asiatica' — 8–12 in, with a wider twisted blade.
  • Vallisneria 'Contortionist' — 10–20 in, with a narrower twisted blade. Background.

products.title: Butterfly Moss
products.body_html:
Moss you can actually see the leaves on. Butterfly Moss (Plagiomnium sp. 'Butterfly') grows rounded, overlapping leaves along creeping stems — wing-like and large enough to read as foliage, where Java Moss and Christmas Moss are a fine green haze. It's the moss to use when you want structure rather than fuzz.

What You’ll Receive

  • Loose Portion: A small loose portion of Butterfly Moss, approximately 2" x 2" in size
  • Ready to Attach: Ideal for gluing or tying to hardscape; will self-adhere over time
  • Note: Occasionally may include a mix of other moss species due to its delicate nature

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Butterfly Moss
  • Scientific name — Plagiomnium sp. 'Butterfly'
  • Placement — Midground, attached to wood, stone or mesh
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Intense light bleaches it and invites algae
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–78°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Note the ceiling — this moss prefers cooler water than most tropical plants
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation — divide and re-attach

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep it under 78°F. Plagiomnium comes from cooler, shaded, damp habitats. In a tank running at 80–82°F it thins out and browns — the single most common reason this moss disappoints. Pair it with cooler-water species rather than discus.
  • The hair-like growths at the base are rhizoids, not algae. They're how the moss anchors itself — leave them.
  • Tie or glue it thinly. Thick mats trap detritus and rot from underneath; a thin layer grows across the surface instead.
  • It is a true moss, not a liverwort, despite the leafy appearance.
  • Slow growth means it holds a shape for months without trimming — useful on a moss wall where faster species need constant cutting.

products.title: Bacopa Platinum Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Almost no green at all. Bacopa monnieri 'Platinum' is the albino form of the toughest stem plant in the hobby — white to palest cream foliage against dark substrate. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format, which matters more here than on most plants: an algae outbreak introduced with the plant is very hard to recover from on foliage this slow and this pale.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture package with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Package size: Approx. 4 inches
  • Sustainable growth aquarium plant species
  • Great value! Nice specimen!
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — White Moneywort, White Water Hyssop
  • Scientific name — Bacopa monnieri 'Platinum'
  • Also known as — Bacopa Platinum
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is pantropical
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 inches
  • Mature height — 6-12 inches
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium to high. Under weak light it stretches thin and pale reaching for more
  • CO₂ — Required. With almost no chlorophyll, it needs every advantage available
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5. Stability matters more than any specific value
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate plus regular water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • White tissue cannot photosynthesize. That is the whole difficulty in one sentence. Plain Bacopa monnieri survives neglect because it produces energy efficiently; Platinum produces almost none, so every other condition has to compensate.
  • It can revert to green. Green shoots photosynthesize properly and will outgrow the white growth if left. Cut them out at the base to keep the stand white.
  • Strong light keeps it low and creeping; weak light makes it stretch and thin. Neither is unhealthy, but only one looks like the photographs.
  • Separate the plantlets and plant them an inch apart, and rinse the gel off completely — on a plant this slow, gel-fed algae in the first weeks is hard to reverse.
  • Also available as loose fresh-cut stems if you want larger plants immediately.

products.title: Hydrocotyle Tripartita Mini
products.body_html:
Half the leaf, half the height. Hydrocotyle tripartita 'Mini' is a dwarf form of the standard clover pennywort — same three-lobed leaves and fast creeping runners, but small enough to stay flat at 1–2 inches instead of climbing. In a nano tank, that difference is what makes it a carpet rather than a shrub.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants or potted plants
  • Fresh-cut plants | loose, small fresh-cut portion
  • Bunched plants | fresh-cut plants bundle with foam and plant's weight
  • Potted plants | fresh-cut plants potted with rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Hydrocotyle, Mini Pennywort
  • Scientific name — Hydrocotyle tripartita 'Mini'
  • Also known as — Hydrocotyle Japan Mini, Japanese Pennywort Mini
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high. Light is what keeps it flat rather than climbing
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners — cut and replant sections

Grower’s Notes

  • Buy Mini for nano tanks, standard for everything else. Full-size Hydrocotyle tripartita reaches 3–4 inches and looks oversized in a small aquarium. The Mini form holds the scale.
  • Light decides carpet or climber. Weak light makes the runners stretch upward, and it stops being a carpet — a lighting problem, not a plant problem.
  • It grows fast. Trim runners every few weeks or it crosses into neighboring plants.
  • Pin fresh cuttings down with weights or tweezers until roots grab; loose sections float free.
  • Every cutting with a node will root, so one portion becomes a carpet in a couple of months.

products.title: Staurogyne Repens White Albino Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Staurogyne repens is one of the most reliable low carpeting plants in the hobby. The 'White Albino' form takes that familiar shape and strips almost all the green out of it, leaving pale ivory foliage that glows against dark substrate. Less chlorophyll means less energy, so it asks for considerably more than the standard form.

What You'll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Staurogyne Repens 'White Albino' plantlets—ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant with care.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — White Albino Staurogyne
  • Scientific name — Staurogyne repens 'White Albino'
  • Also known as — Staurogyne repens 'Variegated'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species comes from the Rio Cristalino, Brazil
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 inches
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium. Note the ceiling — strong light bleaches pale tissue
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious creeping stem
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • Pale tissue burns before green tissue does. Do not treat "needs light" as "needs more light". Medium intensity is the target — strong light bleaches the ivory leaves and algae takes hold on them long before it touches anything green in the tank.
  • Reverted green shoots will appear. Any pale sport can throw fully green growth, and green grows faster. Cut those stems out at the base as soon as you spot them or they will take over the group.
  • Feed the substrate. With reduced pigment the plant cannot afford an inefficient root zone. Aquasoil or root tabs under the planting area make the difference between slow and stalled.
  • Plant small portions, spaced out. Rinse the gel off and separate the culture into groups of two or three plantlets an inch apart. Dense clumps shade their own bases, which this plant recovers from poorly.
  • Want the same carpet without the difficulty? Standard Staurogyne repens is a Beginner plant with the same shape and growth habit — the albino form is a collector's plant, not a workhorse.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Staurogyne Repens Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos shown are sample representations. Actual plant appearance may vary depending on lighting, CO₂, and care. This albino variant is fragile and may melt if not given proper light and nutrients. Not recommended for beginners.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Dwarf Hairgrass | Bulk Pack
products.body_html:
A carpet is built from many small clumps, not a few large ones. Dwarf Hairgrass spreads by runner into a fine, meadow-like lawn — the classic Iwagumi foreground — and this bulk pack gives you 10, 20 or 30 clumps at volume pricing, enough to plant a full foreground in one session instead of waiting months for a single portion to travel across it.

You may know it as Eleocharis parvula. That is the trade name — see the note below.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Dwarf Hairgrass cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Each portion consists of approximately one small clump measuring about 1" x 1" inches.

10 Pack: 10 individual small clumps (approximately 1" x 1" each)

20 Pack: 20 individual small clumps (approximately 1" x 1" each)

30 Pack: 30 individual small clumps (approximately 1" x 1" each)

For best results, separate each clump into smaller portions and plant them a short distance apart to encourage faster carpet formation.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Hairgrass
  • Scientific name — Eleocharis pusilla
  • Also known as — Eleocharis parvula (misapplied trade name)
  • Origin — Australia and New Zealand
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — 10 to 30 clumps, each approx. 1" x 1"
  • Mature height — 3–6 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Why two scientific names?

Dwarf Hairgrass has been sold as Eleocharis parvula in the aquarium trade for a very long time, and most hobbyists still know it by that name.

Eleocharis parvula is a real species — but it is a brackish water plant, not suited to freshwater aquariums. Almost everything sold in the hobby under that label is in fact Eleocharis pusilla, a freshwater species.

So the plant you receive is Eleocharis pusilla: the same Dwarf Hairgrass you have always bought, correctly named, and genuinely suited to a freshwater tank.

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light must reach the substrate for it to carpet rather than stretch
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Dry start works well
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower's Notes

  • Separate every clump before planting. Divide each clump into smaller portions and set them a short distance apart. Spread out, they close ranks faster than an intact clump would spread on its own, because runners only travel into open substrate.
  • Keeping it alive is easy; carpeting it is not. That gap is why this is rated Intermediate. Survival needs little, but a dense low lawn needs strong light at substrate level and usually CO₂ — without both, expect a thin, stretched meadow.
  • Trim the carpet once established. Cutting it back triggers a flush of runners and thickens the mat rather than adding height.
  • Feed at the roots. Runner production stalls without a nutrient substrate or root tabs, and that is what decides how quickly the gaps close.
  • Expect the emersed blades to melt back in the first weeks. New growth comes from the runners, not the original blades — leave it alone through the transition.

Want a shorter, flatter lawn? The Dwarf Hairgrass Mini Bulk Pack stays 1–2 in. Just need one portion? See the standard Dwarf Hairgrass, or the sterile Vitro Culture format.

products.title: Brazilian Pennywort
products.body_html:
Want one plant you can use three ways? Brazilian Pennywort grows planted in substrate, draped over hardscape, or left floating at the surface — and it does all three well. Round coin-shaped leaves on creeping stems, growing fast enough to fill a gap in weeks.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Brazilian Pennywort cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

Fresh Cut Plants: Approximately 4 fresh-cut stems without roots.
Fresh Cut Bunched: Approximately 4 stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
Fresh Cut Potted: About 4 stems potted securely in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Brazilian Pennywort
  • Scientific name — Hydrocotyle leucocephala
  • Placement — Midground, or floating
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required if planted; none needed if floated
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners and stem cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • Floating is a legitimate way to grow it, not a failure. Left at the surface it grows faster, throws roots into the water column and shades the tank below — useful in a shrimp or fry tank. Planted, it grows more upright and compact. Both are correct; choose deliberately.
  • It responds strongly to trimming. Every cut forces branching, which is how a few stems become a bush — and how you keep a fast plant from taking the tank.
  • It strips nitrate quickly, which makes it genuinely useful in a newly cycled or heavily stocked tank.
  • Replant the trimmed tops. Cut stems root within days whether planted or floated.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Balansae Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Cryptocoryne balansae grows like Vallisneria and behaves like a crypt. Long ribbon leaves with a deeply hammered, puckered surface rise a foot or more and sway with the flow — all without CO₂ or strong lighting. It is the low-tech route to a moving green background.

What You'll Receive

  • One (1) Vitro Culture® 4-inch bag of Cryptocoryne crispatula var. balansae
  • Yield: Approximately 3–4 young plantlets, ready to plant into your aquascape

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Balansae Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne crispatula var. balansae
  • Also known as — Crypt Balansae, Cryptocoryne balansae
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 12-20 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • It handles hard, alkaline water better than most crypts. Balansae comes from limestone streams, so it suits tap water that other Cryptocoryne sulk in — a genuinely useful trait if your water is hard.
  • Expect melt, then ribbon leaves. Tissue culture plantlets shed their emersed foliage as they convert. Leave the roots undisturbed; the long submersed leaves start appearing within three to six weeks.
  • The hammered texture develops with age. Young leaves come out relatively smooth. The puckered, quilted surface — the reason to buy this over Vallisneria — shows on mature growth.
  • Root tabs, not liquid dosing. A 12-20 inch leaf takes a lot of energy and crypts draw it from the substrate. Enriched soil or tabs under the crown are what produce full-length leaves.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level and then leave it. Bury the roots only. Every replant restarts the melt cycle, so choose the position before planting and let the runners spread on their own.

products.body_html:
Want the look of Vallisneria from a Crypt? Cryptocoryne crispatula var. balansae sends up long, narrow ribbon leaves with a distinctive hammered, ruffled texture — a background plant that moves like grass but behaves like a Crypt, and one that takes hard water in its stride.

  • Bare-root plants | approx. 1-2 plants loose, bare-root portion

  • Also known as — Cryptocoryne balansae
  • Origin — Southern Thailand
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 12–20 in

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

Miniature conifers in a planted tank. Pogostemon deccanensis — the Indian Star plant — packs fine needle-like leaves densely around upright stems, giving vertical structure no broad-leaved plant can. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format: pest-free, algae-free and pesticide-free.

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple healthy Pogostemon deccanensis plantlets—ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium.

  • Scientific name — Pogostemon deccanensis

  • Origin — Maharashtra, western India
  • Placement — Background, in groups

products.title: Anubias Coffeefolia
products.body_html:
Want texture from an Anubias? Coffeefolia grows deeply rippled, corrugated leaves that look closer to a coffee plant than a typical smooth Anubias — and new leaves emerge bronze-copper before hardening to deep green, so an actively growing plant shows both colors at once.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bare-Root Plants: One Anubias Coffeefolia plant with 4 or more healthy leaves, loose and unpotted
  • Potted Plants: One Anubias Coffeefolia plant with 4 or more healthy leaves, rooted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Coffeefolia Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri 'Coffeefolia'
  • Placement — Midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 6–10 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. As tough as any Anubias
  • Light — Low to medium. Shade suits it; bright light means algae on slow leaves
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower’s Notes

  • The bronze is new growth, not stress. Fresh leaves come in coppery-bronze and darken to green over several weeks. A plant showing bronze at the growing tip is a healthy plant, not a deficient one.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots can go into substrate; the rhizome cannot. Buried, it rots — the most common way an Anubias is lost.
  • The rippled surface traps detritus more than a smooth leaf does. A gentle wave of the hand during water changes keeps it clean.
  • Keep it shaded. Slow growth means algae settles faster than the plant replaces the leaf, and textured leaves are harder to wipe.
  • Divide with a clean blade, keeping at least three leaves per section.

Looking to buy in bulk? Get 10 or 20 plants in one order with our Anubias Coffeefolia Bulk Pack and save 40–50% per plant.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Anubias Care Guide.

Notes

  • Avoid burying the rhizome in substrate to prevent rot. Attach to hardscape for best results. Minor cosmetic leaf blemishes are normal and will improve with new growth in your tank.

products.title: Bucephalandra Kedagang Blue Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Kedagang Blue, also sold as Buce Godzilla Blue, carries dark green leaves with a blue cast that deepens once the plant settles into submersed growth. Kedagang is the plant; Godzilla is the trade name, and color is what separates one Kedagang from another.

What You'll Receive

  • One sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® tissue culture bag
  • Approximately 4 small plantlets grown in sterile nutrient gel
  • 100% free from snails, algae, pesticides and pathogens
  • Rinse the gel away and separate the plantlets before planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Kedagang Blue Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Kedagang Blue'
  • Also known as — Buce Godzilla Blue, Bucephalandra Blue Godzilla
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Too much light brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Deepens color and speeds growth if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; attaches to wood or rock.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Your light source decides whether this plant looks blue. The blue is a surface reflection rather than a pigment. Under RGB or full-spectrum lighting it reads clearly blue-green; under warm white the same plant looks dark green. Check the light before assuming you received the wrong thing.
  • Godzilla means Kedagang. The Godzilla name travels with several Kedagang color forms — blue, red, pink. Same plant type; buy on the color you want rather than the name.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the four plantlets before attaching. Leftover nutrient agar clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.

products.title: Aponogeton Longiplumulosus
products.body_html:
Deeply ruffled leaves that move with the current. Aponogeton longiplumulosus is a Madagascar bulb plant that grows long, flowing, heavily undulating leaves — the ruffling is pronounced enough that the plant reads as movement rather than mass. It grows fast and wants room; 20 gallons is a sensible minimum.

What You'll Receive

At Aquarium Plants Factory®, we offer two options to suit every aquarist's preference:

  • Sprouted Bulb With Leaf – A healthy bulb that has already sprouted and includes at least one leaf for a guaranteed head start
  • Bulb Only Without Leaf – A healthy dormant bulb for experienced hobbyists who prefer to grow the plant from its resting stage

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ruffled Aponogeton
  • Scientific name — Aponogeton longiplumulosus
  • Family — Aponogetonaceae
  • Origin — Madagascar
  • Plant type — Bulb / tuber
  • Placement — Midground to background; best in larger aquariums
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Optional but beneficial
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. Cannot be grown emersed
  • Propagation — Bulb division

Grower's Notes

  • Give it 20 gallons or leave it alone. Fast growth and long ruffled leaves mean a single bulb dominates a small tank within weeks. In a nano it is not a centerpiece, it is the whole scape.
  • Set the bulb on the substrate, don't bury it. Leave the top third exposed; buried bulbs rot instead of sprouting.
  • A dormant rest is normal. Leaves die back, the bulb rests, and growth resumes. Leave it in place rather than discarding it.
  • Root tabs are not optional on a fast-growing bulb plant. It exhausts its own reserves and then stalls in inert gravel.
  • The ruffling shows best with some water movement. In dead-still water the leaves hang rather than flow, which loses most of the effect.

Notes

  • Bulbs without leaves are healthy and capable of sprouting under proper aquarium conditions. Sprouting time varies depending on water parameters, lighting, and aquarium stability. If you're new to bulb plants or prefer immediate results, we strongly recommend selecting the Sprouted Bulb With Leaf option.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Samolus Valerandi
products.body_html:
Miniature lettuce, underwater. Samolus valerandi forms tight rosettes of rounded, bright green leaves that stack outward from a central crown — a leafy, almost vegetable texture that stands apart from the grasses and stems around it. It grows submerged in an aquarium or emersed in a paludarium or riparium equally well.

What You’ll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our versatile selection of high-quality aquatic plants, available in three convenient formats:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Includes approximately 1-2 fresh-cut stems without roots. Perfect for flexible planting arrangements.
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approximately 1-2 fresh-cut stems without roots, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: About 1-2 fresh-cut stems without roots, securely potted in a net pot with rockwool, ensuring stability and healthy growth.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Samolus Valerandi
  • Scientific name — Samolus valerandi
  • Also known as — Samolus parviflorus, Samolus floribundus, Lysimachia parvifolia, Water Mini Lettuce, Water Pimpernel
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 2–6 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Strong light keeps the rosettes compact
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required

  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Grows submerged or emersed
  • Propagation — Side shoots and separated rosettes

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep it under 78°F. Samolus sits at the cooler end of the range and loses compactness in a warm tank. It suits room-temperature setups better than a tropical community running at 80°F+.
  • As a rosette it stays where you put it. No topping, no replanting, no stems falling over — far less work than a stem plant of similar size.
  • Loose, stretched rosettes mean not enough light. Increase intensity rather than dosing harder.

products.title: Dwarf Baby Tears
products.body_html:
The finest carpet in the hobby, and the least forgiving. Dwarf Baby Tears — HC Cuba — has leaves a few millimeters across, so a healthy carpet reads at a scale nothing else matches. It also wants high light, CO₂, and water below 78°F. Get those right and it carpets fast; get them wrong and it lifts off the substrate in sheets.

What You’ll Receive

Select the format that best fits your aquascape:

  • Fresh-cut Plants
    Small loose clusters of HC (approx. 1"x1"), ideal for immediate planting and the most efficient way to establish a healthy HC carpet.
  • Rooted Bunched Plants
    Healthy stems tied with weight for quick anchoring and faster establishment.
  • Rooted Potted Plants
    Fully rooted plants grown in rockwool — the easiest to transition and quickest to carpet.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Baby Tears, HC Cuba
  • Scientific name — Micranthemum callitrichoides 'Cuba'
  • Also known as — Hemianthus callitrichoides 'Cuba' (the older name, still in wide use), HC Cuba, HC
  • Origin — Cuba
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — Small clusters approx. 1"x1", or rooted portions
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast, once established

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Light must reach the substrate, not just the surface
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 68–78°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Note the ceiling — HC struggles in warm tanks
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich soil
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners and stolons

Grower’s Notes

  • Temperature is the overlooked failure. People blame light and CO₂ when a carpet melts, but HC does poorly above about 78°F. In a tank running at 80–82°F for discus or similar, it will not hold — use Monte Carlo instead.
  • Two names, one plant. Most of the hobby knows it as Hemianthus callitrichoides; the accepted name is now Micranthemum callitrichoides. You will see both on shop shelves and in forums.
  • Plant small — three or four leaves per portion, half an inch apart. Large clumps rot in the middle and float off.
  • A carpet that lifts is a rooting problem, not a nutrient problem. Press portions firmly into fine substrate and keep flow off them until they anchor.
  • If this sounds like more than you want, Micranthemum Monte Carlo carpets in similar style with far less demand.

Want to go deeper? Read our carpet plant comparison: Dwarf Baby Tears vs Monte Carlo vs Dwarf Hairgrass.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference only. Actual plant size, shape, and density may vary based on growth stage and tank conditions. Some initial melting may occur during transition.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bacopa Australis
products.body_html:
Want bright green in a tank full of dark plants? Bacopa australis is one of the lightest greens available — small rounded leaves in tight pairs up a fast, bushy stem. It reads almost lime against Anubias and Crypts, which is what makes it useful.

What You’ll Receive

Elevate your aquascape with our premium, convenient formats:

  • Fresh Cut Plants: ~6+ loose, fresh-cut stems (no roots) for flexible layouts
  • Fresh Cut Bunched: ~6+ fresh-cut stems (no roots), bundled with foam + plant weight for easy placement
  • Fresh Cut Potted: ~6+ fresh-cut stems (no roots) potted in a net pot with rockwool for stability and quick start

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Southern Bacopa
  • Scientific name — Bacopa australis
  • Also known as — Bacopa rotundifolia
  • Origin — Southern Brazil and Argentina
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 3-6 in
  • Mature height — 6–12 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light keeps it compact and bushy
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Tolerates a very wide range of hardness
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Thrives emersed in humid setups
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Trimming decides its role. Topped hard and often it stays low enough for a foreground; left alone it reaches a foot and works as background. The same stems can do either job.
  • It is unusually tolerant of water chemistry — soft or hard, acidic or alkaline. If your tap water has defeated other stem plants, this is a good one to try.
  • Every cut branches the stem, so regular topping is what turns a few stems into a dense bush.
  • Replant the trimmed tops rather than keeping bare lower stems.

products.title: Microsorum Trident Mini
products.body_html:
Trident Java Fern, at nano scale. Leptochilus pteropus 'Trident Mini' keeps the narrow forked leaf that gives Trident its name — each blade splitting into finger-like lobes — but stops at 2–4 inches instead of 8 or more. In a small tank that difference is what makes it usable.

Healthy, vibrant Leptochilus pteropus ‘Trident Mini’ cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in multiple planting formats:

Bare-root Plants:
Approximately 3+ leaf portion, loose rhizome with some roots

Bunched Plants:
Approximately 3+ leaf portion bundled with foam and plant weight

Potted Plants:
Approximately 3+ leaf portion, potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Trident Java Fern Mini
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Trident Mini' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 2–4 in

products.title: Microsorum Pteropus 'Needle'
products.body_html:
The finest leaf in the Java Fern range. Microsorum pteropus 'Needle' grows long, narrow, sharply pointed blades — thinner again than Narrow Leaf, so a mature plant reads as a spray of dark green lines rather than a mass of foliage. Same indestructible fern underneath.

What You’ll Receive

  • Loose rhizome | approx. 6 leaf, loose, bare-root, small portion
  • Potted plants | approx. 6 leaf, potted plants with rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Needle Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Needle' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Also known as — Needle Leaf Java Fern
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground, attached to driftwood, stone or decoration
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6 leaf portion, shorter than mature height
  • Mature height — 6–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

Grower’s Notes

  • Why two scientific names? Java Fern was moved from Microsorum to Leptochilus. Both names circulate; the plant and its care are unchanged.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or stone — buried rhizomes rot, and that is how most Java Ferns are lost.
  • Black spots on older leaves are usually plantlets forming, not disease. Let them grow a few leaves and roots, then detach and attach them elsewhere.

products.title: Echinodorus Chocolate Marble
products.body_html:
A sword with markings, not just color. Echinodorus 'Chocolate Marble' carries a heavy blotched pattern across its leaves — irregular dark mottling on green, closer to camouflage than to the even tones most swords show. It grows to full sword size, so it needs a tank with room.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Bare-root Plants, Bunch Plants or Potted Plants
  • Bare-root Plants | loose bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants | rooted plants bundle with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants | rooted plants potted with net pot and rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Chocolate Marble Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Chocolate Marble'
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10–16 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. Brighter light sharpens the marbling
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it speeds growth
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient substrate and root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Root tabs are the whole game with swords. Chocolate Marble takes almost everything it needs from the substrate. In inert gravel with liquid dosing alone it stalls and the marbling fades — which people mistake for a difficult plant rather than a hungry one.
  • Marbling can fade. Like other patterned swords it may push plainer leaves under weak light or thin feeding. Steady light plus root feeding is what keeps the pattern.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level, never below — buried crowns rot.
  • Expect the first leaves to melt as it converts from emersed nursery growth. The second flush shows the real pattern.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. Plantlets form along a mature inflorescence; let each root, then cut it free and plant it separately.

products.title: Echinodorus Rainbow
products.body_html:
Most sword plants give you one color. Echinodorus 'Rainbow' gives you marbled leaves running white, pale green, yellow, pink and red on the same plant — a hybrid derived from Echinodorus cordifolius 'Harbich Red'. It grows slowly and feeds heavily at the roots, so what it asks for is patience and a well-fed substrate rather than difficulty.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 1 individual bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 1 plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 1 plants rooted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rainbow Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Rainbow'
  • Also known as — Dwarf Rainbow Sword
  • Parentage — Derived from Echinodorus cordifolius 'Harbich Red'
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10–16 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient substrate and root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Root tabs are not optional. This is a heavy root feeder — it takes almost everything it needs from the substrate. In inert gravel with liquid dosing alone it stalls and the colors wash out, and people mistake that for the plant being difficult.
  • Slow growth is normal. Rainbow is not a fast sword. Expect a few leaves a season, not a flush of new growth every month — which is also why it stays in proportion in a mid-sized tank.
  • Variegation can revert. Under weak light or thin feeding a marbled plant will often start pushing plain green leaves. Steady light and root feeding are what hold the color.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A settled plant sends up an inflorescence carrying plantlets along its length. Let each grow roots and three or four leaves before cutting it free.

products.title: Rotala Mexicana Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Needle-fine leaves that turn orange. Rotala mexicana carries small, narrow leaves in tight whorls and shifts from bright green to reddish-orange under strong light. The texture is finer than most Rotala, which is what makes it useful for depth and flow in a layout rather than mass.

What You'll Receive

  • One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple Rotala mexicana plantlets, grown in vitamin-enriched gel
  • Tissue culture propagated — 100% free of snails, algae, pathogens and pesticides, so safe for shrimp tanks and nano setups

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rotala mexicana
  • Scientific name — Rotala mexicana
  • Origin — North and Central America
  • Type — Stem plant
  • Foliage — Narrow needle-like leaves in tight whorls; bright green to reddish-orange
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Necessary for the red and orange tones

  • Color depends on light intensity. In medium light it stays green — attractive, but not what the plant is bought for.
  • Plant stems individually rather than as a clump. Fine-leaved stems shade each other badly when bunched.

products.title: Myriophyllum Mattogrossense Golden Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Milfoil in pale gold instead of green. Myriophyllum mattogrossense 'Golden' carries the same fine feathered whorls as the standard species, but under strong light the foliage runs very pale yellow to nearly white, sometimes with reddish tips. It is a striking plant and a demanding one — the color comes from low pigment, which makes it slow to recover and quick to show algae.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Myriophyllum mattogrossense 'Golden' Vitro Culture® grown in sterile laboratory conditions and sealed in 4-inch tissue culture bags.

Choose your preferred pack size:

  • Pack 1 — 1 × 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag containing many small plantlets ready to separate and plant
  • Pack 5 — 5 × 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags, each yielding many small plantlets
  • Pack 10 — 10 × 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags, for larger aquascaping projects

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Golden Mattogrossense Milfoil
  • Scientific name — Myriophyllum mattogrossense 'Golden'
  • Also known as — Golden Watermilfoil, White Milfoil
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Brazil
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — 4-inch bag of small plantlets
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — High. Light intensity is what produces the gold; under medium light it reverts toward green
  • CO₂ — Recommended. Pale foliage photosynthesizes less, so carbon matters more here than on the green form
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0
  • Substrate — Optional. It feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Grown emersed in the lab, converts to submerged growth in your tank
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Put it in a mature tank, not a new one. This is the single thing that decides whether it works. Pale leaves carry little chlorophyll, so the plant cannot outgrow algae — and algae settling on golden foliage destroys the color you bought it for. A stable, established tank with good algae control is close to a requirement.
  • Light decides the color. Strong lighting gives pale gold to near-white with reddish tips; weaker light gives ordinary green.
  • Plant stems individually an inch apart. Fine whorls shade each other badly when a bunch goes in as one lump.
  • Trim and replant the tops. It branches readily from below the cut, and repeated topping builds a dense group.
  • Pair it against dark green or red planting — the contrast is most of the effect. The standard green Mattogrossense is far more forgiving if you want the texture without the difficulty.

products.title: Rotala Orange Juice Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Rotala Orange Juice (Rotala rotundifolia 'Orange Juice') Vitro Culture®

🌿 Key Features:

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Hairgrass
  • Scientific name — Eleocharis pusilla

  • Origin — Australia and New Zealand
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in

Why two scientific names?

Dwarf Hairgrass has been sold as Eleocharis parvula in the aquarium trade for a very long time, and most hobbyists still know it by that name.

Eleocharis parvula is a real species — but it is a brackish water plant, not suited to freshwater aquariums. Almost everything sold in the hobby under that label is in fact Eleocharis pusilla, a freshwater species.

So the plant you receive is Eleocharis pusilla: the same Dwarf Hairgrass you have always bought, correctly named, and genuinely suited to a freshwater tank.

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light must reach the substrate for it to carpet
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Dry start works well
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Divide the cup into many small portions. Plant groups of a few blades an inch apart. Runners only travel into open substrate, so a single lump takes months longer to fill a foreground than the same plant spread out.
  • Keeping it alive is easy; carpeting it is not. That gap is why this is rated Intermediate. Survival needs little, but a dense low lawn needs strong light at substrate level and usually CO₂.
  • Light reaching the substrate decides carpet versus stretch. Shaded hairgrass grows long and thin instead of dense and low.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • Expect the emersed blades to melt back after planting. New growth comes from the runners, not the original blades.

products.title: Utricularia Graminifolia Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want the softest carpet in aquascaping? Utricularia graminifolia — UG — forms a fine, bright green lawn with a fluffy texture nothing else matches. It is also a bladderwort, a carnivorous plant, though its traps are microscopic and target single-celled organisms. It is safe with fish and shrimp, including newborn shrimplets.

What You’ll Receive

One Vitro Culture® portion of Utricularia graminifolia

  • Sold as a 4-inch sealed bag or a 2.5-inch cup, depending on availability (customer cannot choose).
  • Lab-grown in sterile gel/liquid, free from snails, algae, pathogens, and pesticides.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — UG, Grass-leaved Bladderwort
  • Scientific name — Utricularia graminifolia
  • Family — Lentibulariaceae (bladderworts)
  • Placement — Foreground carpet
  • Mature height — 0.5–1 in
  • Growth rate — Fast once established

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 68–78°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Soft water suits it best
  • Substrate — Required. Fine-grain nutrient soil
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Dry start works well
  • Propagation — Stolons

Grower’s Notes

  • Establishment is the hard part, not maintenance. UG commonly melts in the first two to three weeks while it converts from emersed tissue culture growth. Once it has taken hold it grows quickly and needs little from you. Most losses happen in that first month.
  • Stability matters more than any single value. UG reacts badly to swinging CO₂, temperature or hardness — a steady tank beats a heavily dosed one.
  • The dry start method is the most reliable route. Plant into damp soil, cover to hold humidity, and let it carpet emersed for four to six weeks before flooding slowly.
  • Press small clumps into fine substrate rather than planting deep. UG has no real roots — it anchors with fine stolons, which is also why an established mat can lift in sheets if left untrimmed.
  • Carnivorous but harmless. The bladders are a fraction of a millimeter across and catch protozoa and rotifers. Shrimp keepers use UG routinely in breeding tanks.

New to sterile cups? Read our guide on preparing tissue culture plants, or compare options in our Best Carpet Plants guide.

Notes

  • Utricularia graminifolia can be a challenging plant for beginners, as it requires stable water parameters, CO₂, and strong lighting for best results. Pictures are for reference only — plants may vary in size, shape, and color depending on growing conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Wendtii Green Vitro Culture
products.body_html:

This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Wendtii Green Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Green'
  • Also known as — Wendt's water trumpet, Crypt Green
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 4–6 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Tolerates shaded corners other plants refuse
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Hard water suits it, as it does most Crypts
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed

Grower’s Notes

  • The one to start with. Wendtii Green asks less than any other Crypt — no CO₂, low light, and it spreads on its own. If you want to know whether Cryptocoryne suits your tank before buying the harder color forms, buy this one first.
  • Expect melt after planting. Crypts drop their leaves on a change of conditions and rebuild from the roots over two to four weeks. Don't pull them out.
  • Place it once. Every move triggers another melt.
  • Feed at the roots. Root tabs under the crown do more than any liquid dosing.
  • Hard water is no obstacle. Cryptocoryne generally do better in harder water than most planted-tank species — if stem plants have disappointed you in hard tap water, this is the group to try.

products.body_html:
Burgundy that holds without pressurized CO₂. Ludwigia glandulosa, sold widely as Ludwigia peruensis, grows broad pointed leaves in an upright rosette that runs deep green to burgundy red depending on light. It is a North American species and one of the more reliable dark reds in the hobby.

products.title: Rotala Wayanad Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Most red stem plants demand high light, injected CO₂ and a soft-water tank before they show any color at all. Rotala 'Wayanad' is easier than that. It colors from green through orange under medium-high light, and the narrow lance-shaped leaves give a finer texture than the round-leaved macrandra types — closer to rotundifolia in habit, but with warmer tones.

What You'll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Rotala 'Wayanad' plantlets—ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name: Rotala Wayanad
  • Scientific name: Rotala sp. 'Wayanad'
  • Origin: Wayanad district, Kerala, India
  • Placement: Midground to background
  • Shipped size: Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 inches
  • Mature height: 6-14 inches
  • Suits: 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate: Fast

Care

  • Difficulty: Intermediate
  • Light: Medium to high. It grows green under medium light and shifts toward orange and red as intensity rises.
  • CO₂: Recommended. Injection tightens the node spacing and deepens the color; without it the stems grow leggier and stay green.
  • Water: pH 6.0-7.5, 72-82°F (22-28°C)
  • Substrate: Required — a nutrient-rich substrate or root tabs, with water column dosing alongside
  • Growth habit: Upright stems with narrow, lance-shaped leaves and compact nodes
  • Propagation: Cuttings — trim healthy stems and replant the tops

Grower's Notes

  • Trim it hard and often. Fast growth is only useful if you use it. Cutting the group back by a third every couple of weeks forces side shoots and builds the dense bush this plant is capable of.
  • Replant the tops and discard the old bases. Cuttings root within days and outgrow the stumps they came from.
  • Space stems roughly an inch apart when planting. Bundled stems shade each other and rot at the center.
  • Still uncommon outside specialist collections. 'Wayanad' has never been assigned a species epithet and circulates under its collection locality.
  • Expect the emersed-grown tissue culture foliage to melt back before submerged leaves appear. New growth is the honest signal.

products.body_html:

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Below that the stems stretch, lower leaves drop and the color washes out
  • CO₂ — Required. Injection is not optional in practice for this species
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Soft water gives the best color

Grower's Notes

  • This is why the cultured form is worth it. Mature macrandra travels badly — the stems are brittle and the plant resists adapting once it has settled into a particular tank. Plantlets have no such habits to unlearn.
  • Lean nitrate is what brings the color. Fed heavily it grows green whatever the lighting; hold iron and micros steady while keeping nitrate modest.
  • Plant the plantlets separately with an inch of space. Crowded groups shade their own lower leaves and rot at the base.
  • The soft leaves collect detritus wherever flow is weak, and algae follow. Circulation through the group matters as much as light does.
  • Trim and replant the tops rather than letting the stems run. The lower stem goes bare with age, and a replanted top is always the better-looking plant.

products.title: Bucephalandra Red Sword
products.body_html:
A Bucephalandra with a sword leaf. Bucephalandra sp. 'Sekadau Red Sword' grows narrow, elongated, pointed leaves that develop ruffled margins as the plant reaches adult size — a shape almost nothing else in the genus offers. Mature foliage is dark green to olive-brown; the red and pink sit on new growth and leaf undersides, where strong light brings them out.

What You'll Receive

Sold in three formats — choose at checkout:

  • Bare-root Plants: Loose plants with the rhizome and roots exposed, ready to tie onto hardscape with cotton thread
  • Rooted Bunched: Established plants bundled together
  • Rooted Potted: Grown on in a pot, ready to divide or mount

These pest-free, young plants were grown in a lab before transitioning ex-vitro for maximum hardiness. Expect natural variations in their initial size and color as they settle in and mature in your tank!

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Sword Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Sekadau Red Sword'
  • Also known as — Sekadau Red Sword, Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Fast-flowing streams of Borneo
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 3–5 in
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium grows the plant. Strong light brings the red into new growth and undersides
  • CO₂ — Not required. It improves color and pace, nothing more
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed — suits paludariums and Wabi-Kusa
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • This is not a solid red plant. Adult leaves are dark green to olive-brown. The rich red and pink show on new growth and on the undersides, and only when the light is strong. Under low light it still grows well — it just stays green.
  • The sword shape arrives with maturity. Young plants look like ordinary narrow-leaved Buce. The elongated, pointed leaf and its ruffled margin develop as the plant reaches its adult 3–5 inches, which takes months.
  • Tie it on with cotton thread — never glue it. Never bury the rhizome either; buried, it rots. Wrap it onto wood or stone with cotton thread and let the plant grip on its own. There is no such thing as aquarium-safe glue — it is all cyanoacrylate gel, and whatever tissue it touches burns and dies. On a rhizome that is fatal, because a rhizome does not regrow. If you have no choice, a tiny dab on the roots only, where the damage can melt away and grow back.
  • Strong light is a trade-off. It is what pulls the red into the new leaves, but Buce grows too slowly to outpace algae, so a bright position needs grazers, steady nutrients and a watchful eye on the older leaves.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.

Prefer the sterile tissue culture format? See Bucephalandra Red Sword Vitro Culture.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

Notes

  • Bucephalandra species are naturally slow growers and may experience slight leaf melt during initial acclimation. This is temporary — new healthy growth will emerge once conditions stabilize in your aquarium.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Kedagang Japan Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
A Kedagang selected in Japan. Bucephalandra sp. 'Kedagang Japan' carries narrow, slightly rippled leaves with a metallic sheen running green through blue into faint violet. Selected from Japanese stock, where Buce breeding has pushed hardest on color. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

  • One sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® tissue culture bag
  • Approximately 4 small plantlets grown in sterile nutrient gel
  • 100% free from snails, algae, pesticides and pathogens
  • Rinse the gel away and separate the plantlets before planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Kedagang Japan Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Kedagang Japan'
  • Also known as — Buce Japan Kedagang, Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Japanese selection; the genus is native to Borneo
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

  • CO₂ — Not required, though it improves growth and color
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5

Grower's Notes

  • Kedagang is the plant, the suffix is the selection. You'll see Kedagang Red, Kedagang Mini and Kedagang Japan — all the same plant type, differing in color and leaf size. Buy on the look you want rather than assuming they're separate species.
  • The metallic sheen is structural, not pigment — it shifts with viewing angle and lighting, and photographs rarely do it justice.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to rock or wood; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the four plantlets before attaching, or it feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.

products.title: Monosolenium Tenerum (Pellia)
products.body_html:
Thicker than moss, and that is the point. Monosolenium tenerum — Pellia — is a liverwort that grows broad ribbon-like fronds rather than fine filaments, forming dense dark green cushions with real substance. It gives a texture nothing else in a planted tank offers, and it does it in low light with no CO₂.

What You’ll Receive

  • Loose Portion: small portion of Monosolenium tenerum, approx. 2" x 2" (5 cm x 5 cm)
  • Ready for Use: Can be tied to rocks, tucked into crevices, or allowed to carpet over time

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pellia
  • Scientific name — Monosolenium tenerum
  • Also known as — Pellia Moss, Round Pellia
  • Origin — East Asia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on rock or wood
  • Shipped size — Loose portion, approx. 2" x 2"
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light mostly feeds algae on a plant this slow
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic. Does not grow emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation — split a cushion and re-tie the pieces

Grower’s Notes

  • It has no roots and no grip — you must tie it down. Unlike Java Moss, Pellia is brittle and heavy and will not attach itself. Use thread, hairnet or mesh over rock, and expect to leave it several months before it holds. Dropped loose on the substrate it simply drifts apart.
  • Keep the light modest. Slow growth means algae settles faster than the plant replaces tissue, and algae inside a dense Pellia cushion cannot be cleaned out.
  • Give it flow. Water moving through the cushion keeps detritus from packing into the center and rotting.
  • Split and re-tie rather than trimming. Fragments grow into new cushions, so one portion becomes several over a year.
  • Shrimp and fry take shelter in it readily — the dense structure is better cover than fine mosses provide.

products.title: Cabomba Aquatica
products.body_html:
The classic fanwort, in plain green. Cabomba aquatica opens each leaf into a flat fan of fine segments arranged in pairs along the stem — a soft, feathery texture that catches water movement and gives fry somewhere to hide. Easier to keep than the red Cabomba species, and faster.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as submerged fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:
  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approx. 6 stems, loose fresh-cut plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approx. 6 fresh-cut plants bundled with foam and lead weight
  • Potted Plants: Approx. 6 fresh-cut plants with net pot and rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Green Cabomba
  • Scientific name — Cabomba aquatica
  • Also known as — Fanwort, Giant Cabomba
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Under weak light the stems stretch and shed lower leaves
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. Does not grow emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Green Cabomba is the forgiving one. The red and magenta species in this genus demand high light and CO₂ to hold color and drop leaves the moment conditions slip. C. aquatica just grows — the same fan texture, far less argument.
  • Handle it as little as possible. Cabomba stems shed leaves where they're gripped; plant them once, by the bare lower stem.
  • Bottom leaves dropping means light isn't reaching them. Trim the tops and replant rather than letting stems get leggy.
  • It feeds from the water, not the substrate, so liquid dosing does more here than root tabs.
  • Some melting after shipping is normal for the genus. New growth from healthy stems follows within a week or two.

Want to go deeper? Read our guide to growing Cabomba plants.

Notes

  • Cabomba species can be delicate during shipping and acclimation. Some initial melting or leaf drop may occur, but healthy stems will regrow once established.

products.title: American Frogbit
products.body_html:
Miniature lily pads that need no planting. Limnobium spongia — American Frogbit — floats round, glossy leaves on the surface with a curtain of fine roots trailing beneath. Native to North America, undemanding, and one of the few floaters that looks deliberate rather than weedy.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as a small portion – approx. 1–2 individual plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — American Frogbit
  • Scientific name — Limnobium spongia
  • Origin — North America
  • Placement — Free-floating on the surface
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required. It takes CO₂ from the air
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed on wet margins
  • Propagation — Runners — daughter plants form on side stolons

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep the leaves dry on top. Frogbit hates water landing on its leaves — condensation from a tight lid or spray from a filter return makes the tops rot. An open top or a small gap under the lid solves it, and it's the single most common reason Frogbit fails.
  • The long root curtain is the point. It gives shrimp and fry cover and pulls nutrients straight out of the water column.
  • Surface flow packs it into corners. Aim filter returns downward or add a floating ring.
  • Thin it regularly — daughter plants form fast and a sealed surface starves plants below of light.
  • Compare with Amazon Frogbit: similar habit, larger leaves, tropical rather than North American.

Notes

  • As a floating plant, American Frogbit may spread quickly in nutrient-rich water. Regular thinning may be required to maintain light penetration for plants below.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.
