products.title: Rotala Macrandra
products.body_html:
The plant that separates good tanks from great ones. Rotala macrandra carries the largest leaves in the genus — broad, soft and translucent — in a red that runs from rose to deep crimson. It is also the least forgiving Rotala we sell. Light, CO₂ and iron all have to be right at the same time, and the plant tells you immediately when one of them slips.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as emerged fresh-cut plants without root
  • Fresh-cut plants | approx. 6 loose fresh-cut plants
  • Bunched plants | approx. 6 fresh-cut plants bundle with foam and plant weight
  • Potted plants | approx. 6 fresh-cut plants potted with net pot and rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rotala Macrandra
  • Scientific name — Rotala macrandra
  • Also known as — Giant Red Rotala, Rotala Rose
  • Origin — India
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Below that the stems stretch, the lower leaves drop and the red fades to a washed bronze
  • CO₂ — Required. This is the one Rotala where injection is not optional in practice
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Soft water gives the best color
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate plus water column dosing; iron in particular drives the red
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • The leaves are thin enough to be an algae magnet. Soft, broad foliage collects detritus wherever flow is weak, and algae follow within days. Steady circulation through the group matters as much as the lighting does.
  • Lean nitrate is what makes it red. Fed heavily it grows green and leafy no matter how strong the light — hold iron and micros steady while keeping nitrate modest.
  • Trim before it reaches the surface. Once the tops shade the stems beneath, the lower half strips bare and does not recover.
  • Replant the tops and discard the old bases. Cuttings root and color up faster than the stumps they came from.
  • If this proves too demanding, Rotala macrandra 'Green' has the same soft, round-leaved habit without the pigment demand — no iron chase, no color to lose.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Rotala Care Guide.

Notes

  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation. Unless specific, we don't guarantee aquatic plants will be free of pests, pesticides, grow emerged, or submerge.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Anubias Golden (Small Size)
products.body_html:
Bright yellow-green leaves in a genus that is otherwise uniformly dark. Anubias Golden pushes new growth in a golden-lime tone that deepens toward green as each leaf matures. This is the young grade — small now, growing into full size in your tank.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as young, miniature size Anubias Golden
  • Sustainable growth Anubias species
  • Fresh and clean, grow direct from our high technology lab farm
  • Young plants grow in a controlled laboratory environment

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Golden Anubias (Small)
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri 'Golden'
  • Also known as — Anubias Golden Nana
  • Origin — Cultivated variety; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Shade suits it; strong light means algae on slow-turning leaves.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Occasional liquid fertilizer deepens the color.

products.title: Mixed Lotus Seeds – Assorted Colors for Ponds, Water Gardens, and Aquascapes
products.body_html:
Growing a lotus from seed takes about a week to sprout and a season to flower, and the seed itself is the cheapest way into a plant that otherwise ships as an expensive tuber. This is a mixed lot — pink, white, yellow and multi-colored varieties — so you find out what you have when it blooms.

What You'll Receive

  • Scientific Name: Nelumbo nucifera
  • Common Name: Lotus
  • Product Type: Mixed Lotus Seeds (Hardy and Tropical Varieties)
  • Light Requirement: Full Sun
  • Planting Medium: Heavy clay soil or aquatic planting media
  • Germination Time: 1–7 days after soaking
  • Ideal Use: Outdoor ponds, decorative water gardens, patio water containers

How to Grow Lotus Seeds

  • 1. Scarify the seed. Lotus seeds are oval with one pointed end and one rounded end. Do not file the pointed (embryo) end. Instead, gently file the rounded end until you see the white inner layer. This helps water enter the seed and encourages germination.
  • 2. Soak the seed. Place the scarified seed in a container of warm, clean water (around 75–85°F or 24–29°C). Change the water daily to keep it fresh.
  • 3. Sprouting. Within 1–7 days, the seed will swell and a sprout will emerge. Allow the sprout to grow 4–6 inches before planting.
  • 4. Transfer to soil. Plant the sprouted seed into a pot filled with heavy clay soil or aquatic planting media. Submerge the pot under 2–4 inches of water.
  • 5. Growing in water. Place the potted seedling in a sunny, warm location. As it matures, the lotus will send leaves above the water's surface and eventually produce stunning blooms.

Grower's Notes

  • Filing the wrong end kills the seed. The pointed end holds the embryo. File the rounded end only, and only until the white layer shows — going deeper damages what you are trying to germinate. This one step accounts for most failed lotus seeds.
  • Change the soaking water daily. Stale water fouls and the seed rots before it sprouts. Fresh warm water every day for the first week is the difference between a 1-7 day germination and nothing.
  • Do not plant the sprout too early. Wait until the shoot is four to six inches long. Planted shorter, it struggles to reach light through the water and stalls.
  • Lotus needs more sun than a water lily. Full sun all day is the target. In partial sun you will get leaves and no flowers, and lotus leaves are large enough to be worth growing on their own — but flowering needs the light.
  • Expect flowers in the second season. A seed-grown lotus spends its first year building a rhizome. That is normal and not a sign anything is wrong.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Guide on How to Grow Lotus Flowers from Seeds.

Notes

  • While our lotus seeds (Nelumbo nucifera) are selected for very high sprouting rates, we do not guarantee the flower color or that every seed will successfully grow. Flower coloration may vary naturally. Proper care, growing conditions, and patience are essential for best results.

  • Feeding — Regular feeding through the growing season supports the growth rate
  • Overwintering — Tropical. Must be protected from freezing outside tropical climates
  • Propagation — Tuber division

Grower's Notes

  • Check your pond before you buy. Pads spreading over two feet each means a single plant will dominate anything smaller than a large pond. If the 14-inch flowers are what you are after, give it the scale it needs.
  • It rivals the Victoria lilies for size but carries no thorns, which makes it far safer to handle and to keep around fish and wading birds.
  • Flowers to 14 inches, which is extraordinary for a Nymphaea and the main reason people seek it out.
  • Highly fragrant as well as large — the two rarely come together at this scale.
  • Feed generously. A plant producing pads this size runs through nutrients quickly, and flowering suffers first when it runs short.
  • Indoors, treat it as a foliage plant you keep cutting. Nothing stops it going into an aquarium and 20 gallons is the practical minimum, but pads that reach two feet outdoors still push hard for the surface indoors, so trimming is constant rather than occasional. The blooms need full-sun-level light over a long day and rarely appear under aquarium lighting — buy it for a pond if the flowers are the point.

products.title: Nymphaea Moonbeam | Light Blue Tropical Water Lily
products.body_html:
Blue fading into yellow in one flower. Nymphaea 'Moonbeam' is a tropical waterlily whose blooms carry a gradient from soft blue and purple through to pale yellow, on petals that curve distinctly inward. The color blend is unusual — most lilies commit to one hue — and the incurved petals give the flower a folded, textured shape.

What You'll Receive

  • You will get 1 young and freshly harvested water lily tuber
  • All of our water lilies tubers/rhizomes have been inspected before ship out and guaranteed they are viable and perfect to grow in a proper pond environment

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Moonbeam Water Lily
  • Scientific name — Nymphaea 'Moonbeam'
  • Type — Tropical water lily
  • Flower — Gradient of soft blue and purple fading to pale yellow; petals curve pronouncedly inward
  • Foliage — Lush green pads
  • Placement — Ponds, container water gardens and large containers, or tanks 20 gallons and up; centerpiece

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Sunlight — Full sun
  • Water — Warm; it wants tropical temperatures to perform
  • Water depth — 12 to 24 inches
  • Substrate — Heavy clay or loam in a large container, or planted into the pond substrate
  • Planting angle — Tropical tuber: straight up at 90°, crown level with the soil
  • Feeding — Aquatic fertilizer tablets through the growing season
  • Overwintering — Tropical. Lift the tuber before frost and store it frost-free, or treat it as an annual
  • Propagation — Tuber division

Grower's Notes

  • Two colors in one flower is genuinely uncommon. Blue lilies are already restricted to the tropicals; one that shades from blue through to yellow within a single bloom is rarer still. This is a collector's plant more than a landscape workhorse.
  • The inward-curving petals catch light differently across the flower, which is much of the effect — worth siting where you can see it at close range.
  • Resilient against the usual waterlily pests and diseases.
  • Tropical, so it cannot overwinter in a freezing pond. Lift the tuber before frost or treat it as an annual.
  • Wants real warmth. In a cool pond it will sit and do little until temperatures climb.
  • Growing it in a tank works; flowering it in a tank is the hard part. Twenty gallons and up will hold the plant, and the lush pads take off quickly enough that you will be cutting them back on a schedule. The blue-to-yellow gradient appears only under light of sun-like intensity over a long day, which is a great deal to ask of aquarium lighting — outdoors in warm water is where the flowers happen.

products.body_html:
Named for the author of The Tale of Genji. Nymphaea 'Murasaki Shikibu' is a rare tropical day-blooming waterlily carrying white blooms tipped in violet around a golden center, with delicate petal layering, over rounded floating pads that often show light mottling. It opens in the morning and closes by late afternoon.

Grower's Notes

  • White with violet tips. Each bloom opens bright white with the petal tips washed in violet around a golden center — a clean two-tone look that stands out among solid-colored lilies.
  • Opens in the morning and closes by late afternoon, so site it where you will see it during the day rather than in the evening.
  • Zones 9–11 only. Anywhere colder, the tuber must come indoors before frost or be treated as an annual.
  • Wants real warmth at 75–85°F. In a cool pond it sits and sulks rather than flowering.
  • Floating pads shade the water, helping limit algae and giving koi and goldfish cover.
  • Expect to trim if you grow it in a tank. It will settle into an aquarium of 20 gallons or larger, and the mottled pads reach the surface fast enough that thinning them becomes a standing job. The blooms are another matter — they want light at sunlight strength over a long daily photoperiod, so indoors this tends to be a foliage plant and the flowers stay a pond proposition.

products.title: Tropical Water Lilies Packages [Grower's Choice]
products.body_html:
Tropical water lilies are the ones with the big, held-above-the-water blooms — flowers up to a foot across on stems that stand clear of the pad. They need warmth and sun, and outside a warm climate they need lifting before winter. This package is six of them, picked by our growers for your zone.

What You'll Receive

  • This combo package contains 6 different tropical water lilies plants
  • We don't label the species. Randomly pick, can't request a specific species

About This Package

  • Genus — Nymphaea species and hybrids
  • Color — Varies; the mix typically spans pink, red, white and yellow
  • Size range — Varies from small to large growers
  • Selected for — Availability and best performance in your growing zone
  • Use — Ponds, container water gardens, or tanks 20 gallons and up, in warm conditions

Care

  • Sunlight — Full sun or partial shade; at least 6 hours of direct sun per day
  • Water — Warm; tropicals will not perform in cold water
  • Soil — Clay soil, topped with gravel to keep it in place
  • Winter — Tubers must be lifted and stored in moist conditions unless you are in a warm climate
  • Feeding — Aquatic fertilizer tabs pushed into the soil during the growing season

Grower's Notes

  • These will not overwinter outdoors in a cold region. That is the single difference that matters between tropical and hardy lilies. If you cannot lift and store the tubers each autumn, buy hardy lilies instead — they come back on their own.
  • Warm water is as important as sun. A shaded or spring-fed pond that stays cool will produce leaves and few flowers no matter how much fertilizer goes in.
  • The blooms stand above the surface. Unlike hardy lilies, which float their flowers, tropicals hold theirs on stems clear of the water — which is why they photograph so well and why they are worth the extra winter work.
  • Plant the tuber upright, crown exposed. Set it in the center of the pot with the growing point above the soil line, then cap with gravel. A buried crown rots.
  • Use heavy clay soil, not potting mix. Compost floats out and clouds the pond; clay holds nutrients where the roots can reach them.
  • A tank of 20 gallons and up if you grow them inside. Ponds and container water gardens are where most of these end up, but a warm indoor tank at that size suits tropicals well. Blooms are the catch: they need light at sunlight strength for a long stretch each day, and below that the plants put everything into pads. Those pads arrive quickly, so trim them often or the surface closes over.

Planting Instructions for Water Lily

There are two main types of water lilies, tropical and hardy. The differences between tropical and hardy water lilies are a growing habit. Tropical water lilies don't do well in winter. Hardy water lilies, on the other hand, can tolerate the cold. Tropical water lilies tubers must be removed from the pond and stored in moist conditions to come back in the future years. In warm climates, they can remain in the pond.
